feed.title: The Larger World Archive
feed.subtitle: Hidden-world claims, their sources, and what the evidence says.

entry.title: The Velocity of Money
entry.summary: Live debate. How fast money circulates, and why its apparent collapse puzzled economists.

entry.title: The Trillion-Dollar Coin
entry.summary: Documented. A legal loophole proposed in 2011 to bypass a debt-ceiling standoff. The proposal is documented; it was never used.

entry.title: Trickle-Down Economics
entry.summary: Live debate. A nickname for supply-side tax cuts, and a claim about who benefits. The evidence is contested and the term is a slogan.

entry.title: Seigniorage
entry.summary: Documented. The profit from issuing money, and the reason governments can fund themselves by printing.

entry.title: Quantitative Easing
entry.summary: Documented. Central banks created money to buy assets. The policy is documented; its effects are argued.

entry.title: The Phillips Curve
entry.summary: Live debate. Inflation and unemployment trade off — until they stopped doing so in the 1970s.

entry.title: The Laffer Curve
entry.summary: Live debate. Tax revenue is zero at 0% and at 100%, so somewhere in between it peaks. The shape is argued.

entry.title: The Kuznets Curve
entry.summary: Live debate. Inequality rises with development and then falls. The data behind it were thin and the pattern is not general.

entry.title: Zimbabwe's Hyperinflation
entry.summary: Documented. A currency destroyed by printing, with documented causes and documented consequences.

entry.title: The Gold Standard
entry.summary: Live debate. Money redeemable in gold, praised for discipline and blamed for depression. The history is documented; the lesson is argued.

entry.title: The Efficiency Wage
entry.summary: Live debate. Paying above the market rate can raise productivity. The theory is documented; the size is argued.

entry.title: The Easterlin Paradox
entry.summary: Live debate. Richer countries are happier; richer people within them are happier; but growth over time does not raise happiness much.

entry.title: Dutch Disease
entry.summary: Documented. A resource boom that hollows out the rest of the economy by raising the currency.

entry.title: Comparative Advantage
entry.summary: Documented. The clearest idea in economics, and the one most often misstated.

entry.title: The Big Mac Index
entry.summary: Documented. A burger as a currency benchmark. It is a joke that works as a teaching tool and not as a forecast.

entry.title: The 2008 Bailouts
entry.summary: Documented. Governments bought stakes in banks and insurers. The scale and the recovery are documented; the verdict is argued.

entry.title: The Zone of Silence
entry.summary: Debunked. A patch of desert in Mexico where radios allegedly fail and meteorites fall. The explanation is an absence of transmitters and a lot of empty space.

entry.title: The Zodiac Killer
entry.summary: Live debate. Five confirmed murders in California, a set of ciphers sent to newspapers, and a case that has never been closed. Two of the ciphers have been solved.

entry.title: Zion Is Another Matrix
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that the 'real world' in The Matrix is a second layer of simulation. It is an elegant reading, and the filmmakers have described it differently.

entry.title: Zhang Heng's Seismoscope
entry.summary: Documented. A bronze vessel that detected earthquakes and indicated direction. The instrument is described in a text and its principle is understood.

entry.title: Zero and Its Transmission
entry.summary: Documented. The numeral system with place value and zero travelled from India to the world. The route is documented.

entry.title: Zero-Point Extraction
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that usable energy can be drawn from the quantum vacuum. The vacuum energy is real; the extraction is not.

entry.title: Zero-Click Search Extinction
entry.summary: Live debate. More searches now end without a click, because the answer appears on the results page or in an AI summary. Whether that is the death of the open web or an ordinary shift is argued.

entry.title: Zelda's Timeline Convergence
entry.summary: Fiction. The Zelda games are officially split into three timelines that later games merge. The split is documented; the convergence is a fan reading.

entry.title: Zealandia
entry.summary: Documented. A continent of five million square kilometres, 94% of it underwater, with New Zealand and New Caledonia above the surface. It is real, and it was formally described in 2017.

entry.title: The Yuba County Five
entry.summary: Live debate. Five men drove into the mountains after a basketball game and were found dead months later. What happened in between has never been established.

entry.title: You Will Own Nothing
entry.summary: Debunked. A phrase from a marketing essay, read as a policy programme. The essay is real; the programme is not.

entry.title: The Yonaguni Monument
entry.summary: Live debate. A submerged rock formation off Japan has flat surfaces, right angles and a stair-like structure. Geologists read it as natural sandstone; others read it as a worked monument.

entry.title: The Yellow Emperor's Dragon
entry.summary: Fiction. The Yellow Emperor is said to have ascended to heaven on a dragon, taking seventy officials with him. It is a foundation myth of Chinese civilisation, and it has been read as a spacecraft.

entry.title: YAYVIDEOGAMES
entry.summary: Documented. A YouTube channel whose strange, looping videos turned out to be made by a person, not a mystery.

entry.title: The Yangshan Stele
entry.summary: Documented. A colossal stone monument left in its quarry, unfinished, still attached at one edge. It is the best evidence of how such monuments were made.

entry.title: Yang–Mills and the Mass Gap
entry.summary: Open problem. Quantum field theory works, and nobody can prove that its simplest version is mathematically consistent — or that its particles have mass.

entry.title: The XYY Supermale
entry.summary: Debunked. An extra Y chromosome was said to produce aggressive criminals. The claim collapsed when the sampling was examined.

entry.title: XKeyscore and Tempora
entry.summary: Documented. Two bulk-collection programmes disclosed in 2013. Their existence is documented; their scope is partly redacted.

entry.title: Xenotransplantation
entry.summary: Documented. Transplanting pig organs into people. The first living recipients survived weeks to months, which is both a real advance and a long way from a treatment.

entry.title: WorldCorp Enterprises
entry.summary: Live debate. A YouTube channel posting disturbing, disjointed videos with corporate branding. It has never been explained, and it may be art.

entry.title: The Wolfsegg Iron
entry.summary: Debunked. An iron block with a groove was found inside a lignite seam in Austria in 1885 and dated to millions of years. It is a piece of nineteenth-century mining equipment.

entry.title: WIMPs versus Axions
entry.summary: Live debate. Two candidates for dark matter, decades of experiments, and no detection of either.

entry.title: Will Died in Bel-Air
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that Will Smith's character died in the first episode and the series is his afterlife. It explains nothing that needs explaining, and it is a joke.

entry.title: Why We Yawn
entry.summary: Live debate. Yawning is contagious, appears before birth, and has no agreed function. The brain-cooling account is the best supported; the social account explains the contagion.

entry.title: Why We Stood Up
entry.summary: Live debate. Bipedalism is the oldest human trait and the least explained. Several hypotheses compete and none is settled.

entry.title: Why We Sleep
entry.summary: Live debate. Sleep restores something, and after a century of research nobody can say precisely what. The candidates are all supported and none is sufficient.

entry.title: Why We Dream
entry.summary: Live debate. Dreams are vivid, emotional, remembered badly, and unexplained. The leading theories disagree about whether they do anything at all.

entry.title: Why We Age
entry.summary: Live debate. Ageing is not one process. Several mechanisms are well described, no single one explains it, and the interventions that extend lifespan in mice have mostly failed to translate.

entry.title: A White Dwarf as a Weapon
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that a stellar remnant could be steered, or used, as a weapon. It appears in science fiction and in UFO lore; the physics of moving a star is the objection.

entry.title: Where Is Kate
entry.summary: Documented. Weeks of speculation about a public figure's absence, ended by an announcement and a diagnosis. A case study in how rumours fill a vacuum.

entry.title: The Wet-Bulb Threshold
entry.summary: Documented. At a wet-bulb temperature of about 35 °C, sweat stops cooling the body and a healthy adult dies within hours, even in the shade. It is a hard physical limit, and parts of the world are approaching it.

entry.title: Webdriver Torso
entry.summary: Documented. A YouTube channel posted thousands of videos of coloured rectangles and a beep. It was a Google test, and Google said so.

entry.title: Water Shafts and Locks
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that the pyramid's shafts were part of a hydraulic system. The shafts are real; the water is not there.

entry.title: The Water-Powered Car
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that a car can run on water alone, usually by splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen on board. The electrolysis costs more energy than the hydrogen returns.

entry.title: The Watchers of Enoch
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The Book of Enoch describes 200 angels who descended, taught forbidden knowledge and fathered giants. It is apocalyptic literature, and the reading that makes them extraterrestrials is a twentieth-century one.

entry.title: The Watcher House
entry.summary: Documented. A family bought a house in New Jersey and received letters from someone calling himself 'The Watcher'. The letters are documented; the author is not.

entry.title: The Warburg Effect
entry.summary: Live debate. Cancer cells ferment glucose even when oxygen is available. Whether that is a cause of cancer or a consequence is the argument, and the difference matters for treatment.

entry.title: The Wandjina
entry.summary: Debunked. Rock art from the Kimberley shows figures with large white faces and haloes. They were read as astronauts in helmets. They are ancestral beings, painted by the people who still paint them.

entry.title: WALL-E Cannibalism
entry.summary: Fiction. A joke theory that the humans on the Axiom are being fed to each other. The film shows a food dispenser, not a body.

entry.title: The Walking Moai
entry.summary: Documented. How were the Easter Island statues moved? A 2012 experiment showed they can be 'walked' upright with ropes, which matches the island's oral tradition.

entry.title: Voynich as a Cathar Text
entry.summary: Live debate. One of many proposed readings of the Voynich manuscript: that it is a Cathar or heretical text. The manuscript is real; the reading is not established.

entry.title: Voynich Alien Botany
entry.summary: Debunked. The Voynich manuscript's plants do not match any known species, which has been read as evidence of an alien or otherworldly origin. The plants are drawings in a medieval herbal tradition.

entry.title: Voice Identification
entry.summary: Live debate. Recognising a voice is something people do well and can do badly under stress.

entry.title: Vitamin C and Linus Pauling
entry.summary: Debunked. A double Nobel laureate claimed high-dose vitamin C treats cancer and colds. The trials did not agree.

entry.title: The Viral Trigger for Schizophrenia
entry.summary: Live debate. Infections in pregnancy are associated with schizophrenia in the child, and the immune system is implicated. The effect is real and small.

entry.title: Vimanas
entry.summary: Debunked. Flying machines described in Sanskrit epics, read as aircraft. The texts describe palaces and chariots, and the reading is modern.

entry.title: The Video Nasties
entry.summary: Documented. A list of films prosecuted in Britain, and the moral panic that produced it.

entry.title: The Vibrator as a Medical Device
entry.summary: Documented. An electric appliance sold to doctors for a diagnosis that no longer exists. The history is documented and often exaggerated.

entry.title: Vents or Ponds
entry.summary: Live debate. Where did the first chemistry happen: deep-sea vents, warm ponds, or somewhere else? Each setting has a case.

entry.title: Vault-Tec Started the War
entry.summary: Documented. The Fallout games imply that the corporation behind the survival vaults knew the war was coming, and may have caused it. The evidence is inside the games.

entry.title: Varsity Blues
entry.summary: Documented. A college admissions scandal in which wealthy parents paid for fraudulent athletic recruitment. The case is documented in indictments and convictions.

entry.title: Valhalla as Coping
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that Norse afterlife imagery was a psychological mechanism for warrior societies. The texts are real; the function is a reading.

entry.title: The Vaimanika Shastra
entry.summary: Debunked. A twentieth-century Sanskrit text describing flying machines. It was written in this century, not in antiquity.

entry.title: The Upside Down Time-Freeze
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the other dimension in Stranger Things is frozen in 1983. It is an interpretation of a work of fiction.

entry.title: Universal Grammar
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that children are born with an innate language faculty that constrains the possible grammars. It reshaped linguistics, and the evidence for the strong version has weakened.

entry.title: Unfavorable Semicircle
entry.summary: Live debate. A YouTube channel that uploaded tens of thousands of silent, cryptic videos. It stopped, and nobody has explained it.

entry.title: The Uncanny Valley
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that near-human figures provoke discomfort before realism is reached. The intuition is widespread; the experimental evidence is mixed.

entry.title: Ulcers Are Bacterial
entry.summary: Documented. Stomach ulcers were said to be caused by stress and acid. Two Australian researchers found a bacterium living in the stomach lining, were ignored for a decade, and won the Nobel Prize.

entry.title: Uber's Greyball
entry.summary: Documented. Software that showed a different version of the app to regulators and to people the company wanted to avoid.

entry.title: Type 3 Diabetes
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that Alzheimer's is a form of diabetes in the brain, driven by insulin resistance. The mechanism is real; the label is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

entry.title: The Twitter Files
entry.summary: Documented. Internal documents released by a new owner, describing moderation decisions. Their content and their framing are both documented.

entry.title: The Twin Prime Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. There are infinitely many pairs of primes two apart. Nobody can prove it, though we now know there are infinitely many pairs at some fixed distance.

entry.title: Hidden Chambers in Tut's Tomb
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that Nefertiti's tomb lies behind the walls of Tutankhamun's burial chamber, based on radar scans. The scans were repeated, and the chambers were not there.

entry.title: The Turtle's Shell
entry.summary: Live debate. A turtle's shell is its ribcage, grown outward and fused. How that happened without killing the animal is the question, and the fossil record has narrowed it.

entry.title: Tryptophan and Turkey
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that turkey makes you sleepy. Turkey has no more tryptophan than chicken, and the meal is the cause.

entry.title: The Truman Show Delusion
entry.summary: Documented. A delusion in which the patient believes their life is a television show and everyone around them is acting. It is documented, it is rare, and it is named after a film.

entry.title: Troy Was Real
entry.summary: Documented. The city in the Iliad was treated as fiction until a German businessman dug up a mound in Turkey. The site is real; the war is another question.

entry.title: The Trojan Horse as a Ram
entry.summary: Live debate. A proposal that the 'horse' was a siege engine or a ship's figurehead rather than a wooden animal. The poem says horse; the archaeology says siege.

entry.title: T. rex the Scavenger
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that Tyrannosaurus was too slow and too small-eyed to hunt, and lived as a scavenger. The evidence points to an animal that did both.

entry.title: Trepanation
entry.summary: Documented. Boring a hole in a living skull, done for millennia, and sometimes survived.

entry.title: Toon Force
entry.summary: Fiction. The convention that cartoon characters obey comedy rather than physics. It is a description of a genre rule, not a claim about anything.

entry.title: The Tongue Map
entry.summary: Debunked. The diagram showing sweetness at the tip and bitterness at the back. It came from a mistranslation and it is wrong.

entry.title: The Toba Catastrophe
entry.summary: Live debate. A supereruption in Sumatra and a theory that it nearly ended humanity. The eruption is documented; the bottleneck is contested.

entry.title: The Titanic–Olympic Switch
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that the Titanic was swapped with its sister ship for the insurance. The ships' records settle it.

entry.title: TikTok as Psychological Warfare
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that a platform is a weapon aimed at a population. The platform is real and its effects are studied; the warfare framing is not established.

entry.title: The Tic Tac
entry.summary: Live debate. A Navy pilot filmed an object off San Diego in 2004 that looked like a tic tac and appeared to move impossibly. It is the best-documented modern UAP case, and it is still unexplained.

entry.title: Thunderbirds
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Giant birds in Native American tradition and in a famous photograph that turned out to be a hoax. The tradition is real; the bird is not.

entry.title: Thule
entry.summary: Live debate. A Greek navigator described a land six days' sail north of Britain, where the sea became sluggish. Nobody knows which land he meant.

entry.title: The Three Men Ghost Boy
entry.summary: Debunked. A figure in a window in Three Men and a Baby was said to be a dead boy. It is a cardboard cutout of one of the actors.

entry.title: The Third Place
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that cafés, bars, parks and barbers are the places where community actually forms, and that they are disappearing. The concept is well formed; the decline is harder to measure.

entry.title: The Strange Man
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta figure who appears in the background of photographs. The story is fiction, and the photographs are props.

entry.title: The Overton Window
entry.summary: Documented. The range of policies a public will accept, and how it shifts. It is a description, not a conspiracy.

entry.title: The Elevator Tape
entry.summary: Live debate. A surveillance clip said to show something impossible in a lift. The clip exists; the reading does not follow.

entry.title: The Amplituhedron
entry.summary: Live debate. A geometric object whose volume encodes particle-scattering probabilities. It works, and it is not yet physics in the usual sense.

entry.title: Tetris as a Soviet Weapon
entry.summary: Fiction. A joke that the Soviet Union built Tetris as a psychological weapon. It was written by a programmer in 1984, and it was not.

entry.title: Terror Management Theory
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that awareness of death drives people toward cultural worldviews and self-esteem. It has hundreds of studies behind it, a replication problem, and a large theoretical apparatus.

entry.title: The Terracotta Army
entry.summary: Documented. Thousands of life-size soldiers buried with the First Emperor, individually modelled and painted, found by farmers digging a well.

entry.title: Mercury Under Teotihuacan
entry.summary: Documented. Liquid mercury was found in a tunnel under the Feathered Serpent pyramid. It is documented, and it is not evidence of anything exotic.

entry.title: The Ten Per Cent Brain
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that we use a tenth of our brains. Imaging shows activity throughout.

entry.title: The Telephone and Deafness
entry.summary: Debunked. Early telephones were said to damage hearing and cause 'telephone deafness'. The claim did not survive measurement.

entry.title: Ted the Caver
entry.summary: Fiction. A caving diary posted online in 2001, in which a narrow passage leads to something. It is one of the oldest creepypastas, and it was written as fiction.

entry.title: The Technosphere Layer
entry.summary: Documented. The claim that human technology has become a geological layer of the planet, with its own mass and dynamics. The concept is now used in Earth-systems science.

entry.title: Technosignature Pollution
entry.summary: Live debate. The idea that a civilisation could be detected by its pollution — nitrogen dioxide, chlorofluorocarbons, industrial waste — rather than by its radio.

entry.title: The Tecaxic Head
entry.summary: Live debate. A small stone head found in Mexico with features said to be Roman. The object is real; its origin is disputed.

entry.title: The Taylor Swift Clone
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that a celebrity has been replaced by a double. It is the oldest rumour in fandom, applied to a new subject.

entry.title: Tartessos
entry.summary: Live debate. A wealthy kingdom in southern Spain, described by Greek writers, that traded with the Phoenicians and then vanished. Its capital has never been found.

entry.title: Tachyons
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Particles that always travel faster than light. They are mathematically possible and physically absent.

entry.title: Swimming After Eating
entry.summary: Debunked. The rule that you must wait an hour after eating before swimming. There is no evidence for it.

entry.title: Sweet Potatoes Crossed the Pacific
entry.summary: Documented. A South American crop was being grown in Polynesia before Europeans arrived. Someone crossed the ocean with it.

entry.title: Sushruta's Surgery
entry.summary: Documented. A Sanskrit surgical text describing operations including rhinoplasty. The text is real and its procedures were performed.

entry.title: The Superman Curse
entry.summary: Debunked. Actors associated with Superman are said to suffer misfortune. The list is long because the franchise is long.

entry.title: Superintelligence
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The proposal that an intelligence explosion would produce a system beyond human control. The argument is documented; the outcome is speculative.

entry.title: Superdeterminism
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The proposal that quantum experiments violate Bell's inequalities because the settings were fixed in advance. It saves locality and gives up free choice.

entry.title: Sundaland
entry.summary: Live debate. A drowned subcontinent in Southeast Asia, exposed at low sea levels, with a coastline the size of Europe's. It is real; what happened on it is the debate.

entry.title: Sugar and Hyperactivity
entry.summary: Debunked. Sugar does not make children hyperactive. Parents and blinded observers disagree, and that is the finding.

entry.title: Succession as King Lear
entry.summary: Fiction. The comparison between the Roy family and Shakespeare's tragedy is made constantly. It is a useful reading and it is not a hidden source.

entry.title: Sub-Simulation Stacking
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that simulations nest inside simulations, so that our world is many layers down. The argument is statistical, and it has no empirical content.

entry.title: Stuxnet
entry.summary: Documented. A computer worm that destroyed uranium centrifuges in Iran by making them spin at the wrong speed while reporting normal operation. It is the first known cyber weapon to cause physical damage.

entry.title: The Streisand Effect
entry.summary: Documented. An attempt to suppress information draws attention to it. The name comes from a photograph of a house, and the mechanism is now a standard part of online strategy.

entry.title: Stone Softening in the Andes
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that Inca masons softened stone with plant acids to fit it perfectly. The fit is real; the method is not established.

entry.title: Stevie Wonder Can See
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that a blind musician is not blind. It is a joke that has been repeated as fact.

entry.title: Sterile Neutrinos
entry.summary: Live debate. A hypothetical neutrino that interacts only through gravity. Several anomalies pointed to it; the experiments have not confirmed it.

entry.title: Stereotype Threat
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that reminding people of a negative stereotype about their group impairs their performance. It replicated in small studies and largely failed in large pre-registered ones.

entry.title: Stepwells
entry.summary: Documented. Buildings that descend to the water table, and the engineering that made them work in a monsoon climate.

entry.title: Starlink and UFO Panics
entry.summary: Documented. A train of bright lights crosses the sky, and a town reports a UFO. It is a line of satellites catching the sun, and the reports are now a routine part of astronomy outreach.

entry.title: The Star of Bethlehem
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Matthew mentions a star that led the Magi to Bethlehem. Astronomy has offered conjunctions, comets and supernovae, and none of them fits the text without strain.

entry.title: Star Jelly
entry.summary: Live debate. A gelatinous substance found in fields, traditionally said to fall from the sky during meteor showers. The DNA work has found frog and toad, and the rest is slime mould and bacteria.

entry.title: The Stanford Prison Experiment
entry.summary: Live debate. The most famous psychology experiment ever run, and the one with the most documented problems.

entry.title: Stairs in the Woods
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta about flights of stairs found in forests, leading nowhere. It began as an imageboard thread and became a genre fixture.

entry.title: Squid Game Card Colours
entry.summary: Debunked. A fan theory holds that the red and blue cards in Squid Game encode the choice between the games and the outside world. The show's creator has described the cards more simply.

entry.title: Split-Brain Consciousness
entry.summary: Live debate. Severing the connection between the hemispheres produced patients whose two halves seemed to know different things. Whether that means two minds is still argued.

entry.title: Spinosaurus Lifestyle
entry.summary: Live debate. A dinosaur with a sail, a crocodile snout and dense bones, proposed as a swimmer. The 2020 tail find supported it; later work questioned whether it could dive.

entry.title: The Spear of Destiny
entry.summary: Fiction. A spear said to have pierced Christ, and a legend that its holder commands the world. The legend is modern.

entry.title: The Sovereign Strawman
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that a birth certificate creates a corporate 'strawman' separate from the real person, and that a living soul can escape law by naming it. Courts have rejected it in every jurisdiction that has heard it.

entry.title: Sony's Rootkit
entry.summary: Documented. Music CDs installed hidden software that compromised the computers of the people who bought them.

entry.title: The Somerton Man
entry.summary: Live debate. A man found dead on an Adelaide beach in 1948, with a scrap of Persian poetry and an unbreakable code. He was identified by DNA in 2022.

entry.title: Soma
entry.summary: Live debate. A ritual drink praised in the Rigveda, and a botanical identification that has never been settled.

entry.title: Solar Geoengineering
entry.summary: Live debate. Cooling the planet by reflecting sunlight — sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere, or brighter clouds. The physics is understood, the governance is not, and the termination problem is the argument against.

entry.title: The Sokal Hoax
entry.summary: Documented. A physicist submitted a deliberately absurd paper to a cultural-studies journal, and it was published.

entry.title: Sodom and the Airburst
entry.summary: Live debate. A 2021 paper argued that a site in Jordan was destroyed by a Tunguska-like airburst around 1650 BC, and linked it to Sodom. The claim is contested on chronology, geology and identification.

entry.title: The Smiling Man
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta about a man in a suit who dances in the street at night. It is fiction, and it is one of the genre's best-known short pieces.

entry.title: Smile.jpg
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta about an image that drives people mad. The image is a story element, and the story is the work.

entry.title: Smart TV Viewing Surveillance
entry.summary: Documented. Televisions that recognise what is on screen and report it. The feature is documented in patents, settings and research.

entry.title: Smart Cities as Surveillance Grids
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that smart-city projects are a cover for total surveillance. The sensors are real; the total grid is not, and the projects have mostly been smaller and duller.

entry.title: Slender Man as a Tulpa
entry.summary: Fiction. The claim that Slender Man became real because enough people thought about him. He was invented in a forum contest in 2009, and the tulpa claim is part of the fiction.

entry.title: Sleepwalking Violence
entry.summary: Documented. People have committed violence while asleep, and courts have had to decide what that means.

entry.title: Skinwalker Whistling Lore
entry.summary: Fiction. Internet posts claim that whistling at night attracts a skinwalker. The taboo is real in some traditions; the internet version is not.

entry.title: Skinwalker Ranch
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A ranch in Utah with a reputation for cattle mutilation, strange lights and 'portals'. It was investigated by a defence contractor and by a television series, with no published findings.

entry.title: The Simpsons Time Machine
entry.summary: Debunked. The Simpsons appears to predict events. With nearly 800 episodes over 35 years, some of them will match, and the ones that do are the ones that get posted.

entry.title: The Silo Green Screen
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the view outside the silo is a screen. It is an interpretation of a television series.

entry.title: Silk Road Glass
entry.summary: Documented. Roman and later glass found along Asian trade routes, showing how far goods travelled and how technology spread.

entry.title: Shrinkflation and Skimpflation
entry.summary: Documented. Products get smaller or worse while the price stays the same. Both are documented by statistics agencies, and both are hard for a shopper to see.

entry.title: Short-Form Video and Attention
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that short-form video has shortened attention spans. The evidence is mixed, the definition of attention is contested, and the platforms measure engagement, not cognition.

entry.title: Shaving Makes Hair Thicker
entry.summary: Debunked. Shaving does not change hair growth. The stubble only feels coarser.

entry.title: The Shadow Biosphere
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The proposal that life with a different biochemistry exists on Earth, undetected because our methods assume ours. It is a serious hypothesis with one famous failed test.

entry.title: The Seven Cities of Gold
entry.summary: Debunked. Spanish explorers were told of seven golden cities to the north. Coronado found pueblos of stone and mud, and no gold.

entry.title: Serotonin and Depression
entry.summary: Live debate. The story that depression is caused by low serotonin is the most repeated claim in mental health. A 2022 review found no consistent evidence for it, and the argument since has been about what that means for the drugs.

entry.title: The Serotonin Critique
entry.summary: Live debate. A 2022 umbrella review found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin. The argument since has been about what that means for the drugs, and the drugs still work.

entry.title: Seed Oils and Inflammation
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that industrial seed oils cause inflammation through omega-6 fatty acids. The biochemistry is real; the clinical evidence does not support the harm.

entry.title: SCP Is a Real Agency
entry.summary: Fiction. The SCP Foundation is a collaborative fiction wiki. The claim that it is a real agency with real containment procedures is a misunderstanding of a very consistent joke.

entry.title: SCP-096
entry.summary: Fiction. A fictional creature that becomes violently distressed when its face is seen. It is one entry in a collaborative writing project with thousands of them, and it is labelled fiction everywhere it appears.

entry.title: Saturated Fat
entry.summary: Live debate. The central claim of modern dietary advice, and the subject of a long, documented argument.

entry.title: Satoshi as an Intelligence Agency
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator was a state intelligence operation. The identity is unknown, and the claim is an inference from the design.

entry.title: The Saraswati River
entry.summary: Live debate. A river praised in the Vedas and identified by some with a dry channel in Haryana. The palaeochannel is real; the identification is argued.

entry.title: The Sanjeevani Plant
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A life-restoring herb from the Ramayana, and a long search for its botanical identity.

entry.title: Salting Carthage
entry.summary: Debunked. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, and the story says the ground was sown with salt so nothing would grow. The salt is a modern invention.

entry.title: Saki Sanobashi
entry.summary: Fiction. A lost anime said to show children trapped in a bathroom. It has never been found, and the search suggests it never existed.

entry.title: The Sailing Stones
entry.summary: Documented. Rocks on a dry lake bed leave long tracks, apparently moving on their own. The explanation — ice sheets pushed by light wind — was confirmed with GPS and time-lapse in 2014.

entry.title: Sai Baba's Miracles
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A figure credited with materialising objects and knowing the future. The claims are testimony; the demonstrations are not testable.

entry.title: Sad Satan
entry.summary: Live debate. A 2015 horror game distributed through the deep web, said to contain illegal material. The claims are unverified, the game has been examined, and its authorship is unknown.

entry.title: The Russian Sleep Experiment
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta about a Soviet experiment that kept prisoners awake for fifteen days. It is written as a report and it is entirely invented.

entry.title: The Roza Bal Tomb
entry.summary: Debunked. A shrine in Srinagar said to be a prophet's tomb. The identification is modern, and the site's own tradition is different.

entry.title: Rothschild Banking Myths
entry.summary: Debunked. A family of bankers has been at the centre of conspiracy theories for two centuries. The theories are documented as theories, and they are false — and they repeat a familiar pattern of antisemitic tropes.

entry.title: Roswell Was Project Mogul
entry.summary: Documented. The 1947 Roswell debris was a secret balloon array built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The US Air Force said so in 1994, and the alien story arrived decades later.

entry.title: The Rosenhan Study
entry.summary: Live debate. Healthy people admitted to psychiatric hospitals and diagnosed. The study reshaped psychiatry and its data have been questioned.

entry.title: Room 641A
entry.summary: Documented. A room in an AT&T switching centre in San Francisco, built for the NSA, where internet traffic was copied. A technician's evidence exposed it in 2006.

entry.title: Rongorongo
entry.summary: Documented. A script from Easter Island, carved on wooden tablets, and undeciphered. Only about two dozen objects survive.

entry.title: Rome Traded with India
entry.summary: Documented. Roman coins are found in India, and a Roman-era text describes the monsoon route. The trade was large enough to worry Roman writers.

entry.title: Roman Dodecahedrons
entry.summary: Live debate. Hollow bronze objects with twelve pentagonal faces and knobs at the corners, found across the northern provinces. Nobody knows what they were for.

entry.title: The Robbers Cave Experiment
entry.summary: Live debate. Two groups of boys at a summer camp were set against each other. The conflict and the reconciliation are both documented.

entry.title: RNA World or Metabolism First
entry.summary: Live debate. Two answers to how life began: a self-replicating molecule, or a self-sustaining chemical network. Both have support and neither is demonstrated.

entry.title: RLHF
entry.summary: Documented. The technique that turned raw models into assistants, and the argument about what it actually does.

entry.title: Richard III Under a Car Park
entry.summary: Documented. The last Plantagenet king was buried in a friary that became a car park. His skeleton was found in 2012, under a marked parking bay.

entry.title: Retrocausality
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that later events can influence earlier ones. Some interpretations use it; no experiment has shown it.

entry.title: Repressed Memory
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that traumatic memories can be pushed out of awareness and recovered later, often in therapy. The evidence for the mechanism is weak, and the recovered memories have produced both convictions and miscarriages of justice.

entry.title: The Replication Crisis
entry.summary: Documented. Large numbers of published findings in psychology and medicine failed to replicate. The failure is documented, and so are its causes.

entry.title: Rendering Optimisation
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that reality only renders what is observed, as a game engine does. The observation is real; the engine is a metaphor.

entry.title: Relational Quantum Mechanics
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that quantum states are always relative to an observer, and that there is no observer-independent description.

entry.title: The Referee Who Bet
entry.summary: Documented. Match officials have bet on games and, in some cases, influenced them. The cases are documented in court and league records.

entry.title: Reality Shifting
entry.summary: Debunked. A practice, spread on TikTok, of moving consciousness to another reality by relaxing into sleep. It is a description of dreaming with a different vocabulary and a stronger claim.

entry.title: Rare Earth or Mediocrity
entry.summary: Live debate. Is complex life rare because Earth is unusual, or ordinary because the galaxy is vast? Both arguments are principled and neither is settled.

entry.title: Randonautica
entry.summary: Debunked. An app that generates a random coordinate and sends you there, promising 'anomalies'. In 2020 two teenagers following one found a suitcase containing human remains, and the app became famous for the wrong reason.

entry.title: Rama Setu
entry.summary: Live debate. A chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka, sacred in one account and a natural feature in another.

entry.title: Raining Animals
entry.summary: Documented. Reports of fish, frogs and other animals falling from the sky are documented across centuries. The mechanism is meteorological, and it is well understood.

entry.title: The Rainbow Warrior
entry.summary: Documented. French intelligence officers sank a Greenpeace ship in Auckland harbour, killing a photographer. France initially denied it, then admitted it.

entry.title: Ragnarök and 536 AD
entry.summary: Live debate. A volcanic winter darkened the sun for eighteen months, and Norse legend describes a winter with no summer. The parallel is suggestive.

entry.title: The Quimbaya Aeroplanes
entry.summary: Debunked. Small gold figurines from Colombia have triangular wings and a vertical tail. Replicas have been flown as gliders, which is the argument, and the argument is backwards.

entry.title: Quetzalcoatl the Visitor
entry.summary: Debunked. A feathered serpent god was recast in the twentieth century as a pale-skinned teacher from overseas. The evidence for the visitor is a sixteenth-century text read backwards.

entry.title: Quantum Tunnelling in Smell
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that we smell by detecting molecular vibrations through quantum tunnelling, rather than by shape. The evidence is mixed and the debate is live.

entry.title: Quantum Coherence in Photosynthesis
entry.summary: Live debate. Light-harvesting complexes were reported to sustain quantum coherence for hundreds of femtoseconds. Whether that coherence helps, or is a by-product, is the argument.

entry.title: Qin's Mercury Rivers
entry.summary: Live debate. The First Emperor's tomb is said to contain rivers of mercury under a ceiling of pearls. The soil around the mound shows elevated mercury, and the tomb has never been opened.

entry.title: QBism
entry.summary: Live debate. An interpretation in which the quantum state is a person's expectation, not a fact about the world.

entry.title: Pytheas in the Arctic
entry.summary: Documented. A Greek navigator sailed to Britain, described sea ice and a frozen sea, and was disbelieved for centuries.

entry.title: The Pyramid as a Pump
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that the Great Pyramid was a hydraulic machine. The chambers and shafts are real; the machinery is not.

entry.title: Purdue and OxyContin
entry.summary: Documented. A company marketed an addictive opioid as low-risk, using a claim about its formulation that was not supported. The consequences are measured in deaths.

entry.title: Puma Punku Laser Cuts
entry.summary: Debunked. Stone blocks at Tiwanaku have precise right angles and interlocking shapes, said to require lasers. They were cut with stone tools, and the site has been heavily disturbed.

entry.title: Publication Bias
entry.summary: Documented. Studies that find nothing are less likely to be published, so the literature overstates effects. The bias is measured, not suspected.

entry.title: How Pterosaurs Took Off
entry.summary: Live debate. Pterosaurs were the size of giraffes and flew. The leading explanation is a quadrupedal launch, using the wings as front legs to vault into the air.

entry.title: The Proton Radius Puzzle
entry.summary: Live debate. Two ways of measuring the proton gave different answers for years. The discrepancy has largely closed, and the episode is instructive.

entry.title: Prompt Injection
entry.summary: Documented. Instructions hidden in text that an AI system reads, which hijack what it does. The vulnerability is documented and unsolved.

entry.title: Prometheus the Rebel
entry.summary: Fiction. A Titan stole fire for humanity and was punished. The story has been read as an account of a visitor who gave technology to humans. It is a myth about knowledge and its cost.

entry.title: Project Azorian
entry.summary: Documented. The CIA built a ship to lift a sunken Soviet submarine from the Pacific floor, and told the world it was mining manganese. It is the most expensive covert engineering project of the Cold War.

entry.title: Project 112 and SHAD
entry.summary: Documented. The US military tested biological and chemical agents on ships and in the open, sometimes without informing the personnel involved. The programme was disclosed decades later.

entry.title: Prion-Like Spread
entry.summary: Live debate. Misfolded proteins that propagate through the brain, implicated in several neurodegenerative diseases. The mechanism is documented for prions; its reach is argued.

entry.title: The Princes in the Tower
entry.summary: Live debate. Two boys disappeared in the Tower of London in 1483, and their uncle took the throne. Bones found in 1674 were never conclusively identified.

entry.title: Predictive Policing Bias
entry.summary: Documented. Systems that send police where crime data says crime happens, which is where police have been sent before.

entry.title: Predictive Coding
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that the brain is a prediction machine, constantly modelling the world and correcting the errors. It explains a lot and has been hard to prove.

entry.title: Predatory Journals
entry.summary: Documented. Journals that charge authors and publish without real review. The category is documented and its boundaries are argued.

entry.title: Power Posing
entry.summary: Live debate. Standing confidently was said to change your hormones and your risk appetite. The hormonal claim did not replicate.

entry.title: Portal and Half-Life Share a Universe
entry.summary: Documented. Two Valve games set in the same world, with a research ship, a shadowy corporation and a shared apocalypse. The connection is documented in the games and confirmed by the studio.

entry.title: The Poolrooms
entry.summary: Fiction. An endless complex of tiled pools and corridors, invented on an imageboard. It is a liminal-space fiction, and it is labelled as one.

entry.title: Pompeii and Herculaneum
entry.summary: Documented. Two towns buried by Vesuvius, preserving streets, food, graffiti and a library of carbonised scrolls.

entry.title: Polywater
entry.summary: Debunked. A form of water said to be denser and more viscous, with extraordinary properties. It was contaminated ordinary water.

entry.title: Polyvagal Theory
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A theory that the vagus nerve supports three hierarchical states — social engagement, fight-or-flight, shutdown — and that trauma traps people in the lower ones. It is enormously popular in therapy and weakly supported in physiology.

entry.title: Polynesian Navigation
entry.summary: Documented. Polynesians settled the Pacific without instruments, using stars, swells, birds and clouds. The claim that they did it deliberately was dismissed for centuries and then demonstrated.

entry.title: The Polygraph
entry.summary: Live debate. A machine that measures stress and is said to detect lies. It measures stress.

entry.title: The Poltergeist Curse
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Several people associated with the Poltergeist films died young, and the deaths are said to be a curse. The list is selected, and the films used real skeletons.

entry.title: The Pokémon War
entry.summary: Fiction. A single line about a war, and a theory that Kanto was devastated by one. The line exists; the war does not.

entry.title: The Pokémon Coma
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that Ash is in a coma and the series is his dream. It has no support in the show and it can be applied to anything.

entry.title: Poe's Law
entry.summary: Documented. Without a clear marker of intent, a parody of extremism is indistinguishable from the real thing. It was formulated on a forum and has been demonstrated repeatedly since.

entry.title: When Plate Tectonics Began
entry.summary: Live debate. The Earth's surface moves in plates, and nobody knows when that started. Estimates range from four billion years ago to seven hundred million.

entry.title: Plant Neurobiology
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Plants signal, remember in a loose sense, and respond to damage. The claim that they have nervous systems, or brains, is where the metaphor stops being useful.

entry.title: Placebo Mechanisms
entry.summary: Live debate. The placebo effect is real, and it is not one thing: expectation, conditioning, regression and reporting bias all contribute, and the size depends on the outcome.

entry.title: Pikachu's Tail
entry.summary: Debunked. A generation remembers Pikachu with a black tip on its tail. It has never had one, and the false memory is a textbook case.

entry.title: The Picts
entry.summary: Documented. The painted people of northern Scotland, known from carved stones and a king-list, whose language left almost nothing.

entry.title: Phrenology
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that personality could be read from the shape of the skull. It was wrong, and it seeded real neuroscience.

entry.title: The Phoenix
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A bird that dies and is reborn from its ashes. The motif is ancient; the bird is not.

entry.title: Phoebe Is Homeless
entry.summary: Fiction. The joke theory that Phoebe in Friends is homeless and sleeps in the coffee shop. It is contradicted by the show, and it is funny.

entry.title: The Phantom Cosmonaut Tapes
entry.summary: Live debate. Recordings said to capture dying Soviet cosmonauts. The recordings exist; the interpretation has never been verified.

entry.title: The PFAS Cover-Up
entry.summary: Documented. Chemical companies knew about the health effects of persistent compounds decades before regulators acted. The documents are public.

entry.title: Petscop
entry.summary: Fiction. A YouTube series presenting footage of a nonexistent 1990s PlayStation game. The game was never made, and the story is in the editing.

entry.title: The Peter Principle
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that people rise to their level of incompetence. It is a joke with a testable prediction, and the tests have been mixed.

entry.title: Peopling of the Americas
entry.summary: Live debate. People reached the Americas before the last glacial maximum or after it, by land or by coast. The dates have been moving earlier for thirty years.

entry.title: The Pentagon's UAP Programme
entry.summary: Documented. A defence department programme to investigate unidentified objects, disclosed in 2017 and later renamed and expanded.

entry.title: Penrose's Cycles
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The proposal that the universe repeats in aeons, with evidence claimed in the cosmic microwave background. The claims have not held.

entry.title: The Peltzman Effect
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that safety features cause people to take more risks, cancelling out the benefit. The mechanism is real; the size of the effect is disputed.

entry.title: Pegasus Zero-Click
entry.summary: Documented. Spyware that infects a phone without any interaction, sold to governments. The 2021 Pegasus Project documented its use against journalists, lawyers and activists.

entry.title: Peer Review's Evidence Base
entry.summary: Live debate. Peer review is the gatekeeping ritual of science, and the evidence that it works is thinner than most people assume.

entry.title: The Patomskiy Crater
entry.summary: Live debate. A cone-shaped mound in the Siberian forest, with a ring of smaller mounds around it. It has been attributed to a meteorite, a gas explosion and a volcano.

entry.title: The Infection Hypothesis of Parkinson's
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that Parkinson's begins with an infection or an environmental trigger that travels to the brain. The pathology spreads in a pattern that fits, and the trigger has not been found.

entry.title: Paper Mills
entry.summary: Documented. Organisations that sell authorship on fabricated papers. Their output is documented in the published record.

entry.title: PANDAS and PANS
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that a streptococcal infection can trigger sudden obsessive-compulsive symptoms in children. The clinical phenomenon is described; the autoimmune mechanism is not established.

entry.title: The Pale King's Rebirth
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory about the fate of a ruler in a game. It is an interpretation of a fiction.

entry.title: Paititi
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A lost Inca city said to lie east of the Andes. Expeditions have searched; nothing has been found.

entry.title: The P2 Lodge
entry.summary: Documented. A Masonic lodge in Italy recruited generals, ministers and intelligence chiefs, and was exposed in 1981. Its members were involved in the decade's political violence.

entry.title: P versus NP
entry.summary: Open problem. Is every problem whose answer can be checked quickly also solvable quickly? Almost everyone believes not, and nobody can prove it.

entry.title: P-Hacking
entry.summary: Documented. Analysing data in many ways until a result appears, and reporting only that. The practice is documented and measurable.

entry.title: ‘Oumuamua as Hydrogen Ice
entry.summary: Live debate. An explanation for the object's odd acceleration: it was a chunk of hydrogen ice. Elegant, and hard to test now that it has gone.

entry.title: ‘Oumuamua's Composition
entry.summary: Live debate. The first known interstellar object, and a shape and acceleration that several explanations fit and none settles.

entry.title: Ötzi's Murder
entry.summary: Documented. A man who died in the Alps 5,300 years ago was found in 1991 with an arrowhead in his shoulder. His last days have been reconstructed in detail.

entry.title: The Orion Correlation
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that the three pyramids at Giza are laid out to match the belt of Orion. The pattern is approximate, the dates do not line up, and the layout has a simpler explanation.

entry.title: Orch-OR
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that consciousness arises from quantum computation in microtubules inside neurons. It has a testable prediction, one experiment that claimed to support it, and no replication.

entry.title: Oppenheimer's Chain Reaction
entry.summary: Fiction. The film dramatises a fear that the first test might ignite the atmosphere. The fear was real, the calculation was done, and the answer was no.

entry.title: Operation Snow White
entry.summary: Documented. The Church of Scientology ran a systematic infiltration of US government offices to remove documents about itself. Eleven senior officials were convicted.

entry.title: Operation Highjump
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A US naval expedition to Antarctica in 1946–47, with 4,700 men and a carrier. It has been read as a military operation against a hidden Nazi or alien base.

entry.title: Open Weights
entry.summary: Live debate. Models released for anyone to run. The benefits and the risks are both documented, and the argument is live.

entry.title: One Piece and the All Blue
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory about where a legendary sea is. It is an interpretation of a long-running manga.

entry.title: The Olmec Heads as Africans
entry.summary: Debunked. The colossal stone heads of the Olmec show faces with broad noses and full lips, and have been said to depict Africans. They depict Olmec rulers, and the stone came from local quarries.

entry.title: Ollantaytambo Machining
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that Inca stonework at Ollantaytambo shows machine cutting. The precision is real; the machines are not.

entry.title: Odd Perfect Numbers
entry.summary: Open problem. A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors. Every one known is even, and nobody knows whether an odd one exists.

entry.title: Ocean Worlds Are the Norm
entry.summary: Live debate. Europa, Enceladus, Titan, Ganymede, Ceres: subsurface oceans may be common. Whether they are habitable is another question.

entry.title: Oannes
entry.summary: Fiction. A Babylonian priest described a fish-man who came out of the sea and taught civilisation. It is a myth recorded centuries after the fact, and it has become a fixture of the ancient-astronaut literature.

entry.title: The NPC Theory
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The joke-theory that most people are non-player characters with no inner life. It began as a meme, and a survey found a surprising number of people willing to say they doubted others' consciousness.

entry.title: Novel Reading and Madness
entry.summary: Debunked. Novels were said to corrupt young women and drive them mad. The claim is documented; the evidence never existed.

entry.title: Non-Human Biologics
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A 2023 congressional hearing was told the United States holds craft and biological material of non-human origin. The claim is consequential, the evidence has not been produced, and the official investigations have found nothing to support it.

entry.title: NoEnd House
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta about a haunted house with a series of rooms and no exit. It is fiction, and its structure has been widely copied.

entry.title: The Ninth Legion
entry.summary: Live debate. A Roman legion stationed in Britain disappears from the record, and has been sent to Scotland, annihilated, or transferred. The evidence points to the dull answer.

entry.title: The Ningen
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A Japanese internet cryptid: a white, humanoid whale said to live in Antarctic waters. It appears to have been invented online.

entry.title: Nibiru
entry.summary: Debunked. A claimed planet on a long orbit that would pass Earth. It has been predicted repeatedly and has never appeared.

entry.title: The Newport Tower
entry.summary: Debunked. A stone tower in Rhode Island said to be a medieval Norse church. The mortar dates it to the colonial period.

entry.title: Newgrange and the Solstice
entry.summary: Documented. A passage tomb in Ireland aligned so that the rising sun at midwinter reaches the chamber floor. The alignment is measured every year.

entry.title: New Coke as a Trojan Horse
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Coca-Cola replaced its recipe in 1985, the public revolted, and the original returned in 79 days. The claim is that the whole thing was a planned manoeuvre.

entry.title: Nessie as a Plesiosaur
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The Loch Ness Monster is usually drawn as a plesiosaur. That identification has a specific problem: a breeding population of large air-breathing reptiles in a cold lake would leave traces, and none has been found.

entry.title: NESARA and GESARA
entry.summary: Debunked. A claimed law that would cancel all debt, abolish income tax and deliver prosperity packages. It has been 'about to be announced' for thirty years.

entry.title: Nero and the Fire
entry.summary: Debunked. Nero was said to have fiddled while Rome burned, and to have started the fire to clear space for his palace. The first is impossible and the second is unlikely.

entry.title: The Nephilim
entry.summary: Fiction. Genesis mentions giants called Nephilim in a handful of verses. The enormous literature built on them — bloodlines, hybrids, modern sightings — is later, and the verses are not a description of a species.

entry.title: Neolithic Trepanation
entry.summary: Documented. Skulls with holes cut into them, and bone regrowth showing that some people survived. The surgery is documented; the motive is not.

entry.title: Nemo Means Nobody
entry.summary: Documented. The name in Finding Nemo means 'nobody' in Latin, which is either a coincidence or the film's central joke. The etymology is documented; the intent is not.

entry.title: Why the Neanderthals Went
entry.summary: Live debate. They lived in Europe for hundreds of thousands of years and disappeared within a few thousand of our arrival. The cause is still argued.

entry.title: Neanderthal Cannibalism
entry.summary: Documented. Bones from several Neanderthal sites carry cut marks and fractures consistent with butchery. The evidence is direct, and the interpretation is not.

entry.title: Near-Death Experiences as DMT Release
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that the brain releases DMT at death, producing the tunnel, the light and the life review. The resemblance is real; the release has never been measured.

entry.title: The Nazca Lines as Water Maps
entry.summary: Live debate. The lines may mark routes to water rather than sky gods or runways. The puquios — spiral wells — are real, and the lines' relationship to them is argued.

entry.title: Nazca Lines as Runways
entry.summary: Debunked. The lines and figures on the Nazca desert were said to be landing strips for aircraft. They are shallow scrapes in the surface, and the ground beneath them would not support a wheel.

entry.title: Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness
entry.summary: Open problem. The equations that describe fluid flow are used every day and have never been proved to have solutions that stay smooth. Turbulence is the reason it matters.

entry.title: Nan Madol
entry.summary: Documented. A city built on artificial islets from stacked basalt columns, in a lagoon in Micronesia. It is real, and it took centuries.

entry.title: N-Rays
entry.summary: Debunked. A French physicist discovered a new radiation that only he could detect. It did not exist.

entry.title: The Mystery Flesh Pit
entry.summary: Fiction. A worldbuilding project about a national park inside a living organism. It is fiction, presented as an archive of a place that never existed.

entry.title: MyHouse.wad
entry.summary: Fiction. A Doom level released with a story about a friend who died. It is a work of art in a 1993 game engine, and it is fiction.

entry.title: The Mushroom War
entry.summary: Documented. Adventure Time is set a thousand years after a nuclear war, and the show reveals it slowly. The backstory is documented in the episodes, not invented by fans.

entry.title: Muppet Citizenship
entry.summary: Fiction. A joke that the Muppets are legally citizens with rights. It is a joke about puppets, and it is filed as one.

entry.title: The Multiverse
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that our universe is one of many. It follows from some theories and has no direct test.

entry.title: MSG Syndrome
entry.summary: Debunked. A letter to a medical journal created a condition. Blinded trials did not find it.

entry.title: Mr Blue Eyes
entry.summary: Fiction. A minor character read as the series' hidden controller. It is an interpretation of a game.

entry.title: The Mozart Effect
entry.summary: Debunked. Listening to Mozart was said to raise IQ. It raises arousal for about fifteen minutes, and the IQ claim was a press release that outlived the paper.

entry.title: The Moving Sofa Problem
entry.summary: Open problem. The largest sofa that can be moved round a right-angled corridor. The best known answer has stood since 1992 and is not proved optimal.

entry.title: The Monument Mythos
entry.summary: Fiction. An analog horror series in which American monuments are something other than monuments.

entry.title: The Montauk Project
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claimed secret programme at a decommissioned radar station on Long Island: mind control, time travel, and a boy who conjured a monster. The station is real; the programme exists only in books.

entry.title: Monsanto's Ghostwritten Studies
entry.summary: Documented. Internal documents showed the company drafting research on its own products and arranging for academics to publish it.

entry.title: Monopoly's Anti-Monopoly Origin
entry.summary: Documented. The world's most famous property game was invented to teach that land monopolies are unjust. The irony is documented in patents and in the inventor's own words.

entry.title: The Mongolian Death Worm
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A worm said to live in the Gobi, capable of spitting venom or electricity. The reports come from travellers, and no specimen has ever been produced.

entry.title: The Momo Panic
entry.summary: Debunked. A bird-woman image was said to be contacting children on WhatsApp and instructing them to harm themselves. It was a sculpture, a hoax, and a lesson in how a panic travels.

entry.title: Mokele-mbembe
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A large animal said to live in the Congo basin, often described as a sauropod dinosaur. Expeditions have been going for a century and have produced stories, not specimens.

entry.title: The Mohenjo-daro Blast
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that an ancient city was destroyed by an atomic blast. The 'evidence' is a scattered set of bones and a misread verse.

entry.title: The Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro
entry.summary: Documented. A bronze figurine from the Indus cities, and a name that tells you more about its finders than its subject.

entry.title: Model Welfare
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The question of whether AI systems can suffer. The question is serious; the evidence is absent.

entry.title: Model Collapse
entry.summary: Live debate. Training on model output is said to degrade models. The phenomenon is documented in some settings; the generality is argued.

entry.title: Mithras and Precession
entry.summary: Live debate. A claim that Mithraic iconography encodes the precession of the equinoxes. The imagery is real; the astronomy is a reading.

entry.title: Mirror Neurons
entry.summary: Live debate. Neurons that fire both when a monkey acts and when it watches the same action. They were found in macaques, and the human claims built on them — empathy, language, autism — are much larger than the evidence.

entry.title: The Minotaur as Earthquake
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that the Minotaur myth encodes a memory of the Thera eruption or of Cretan earthquakes. The myth is real; the encoding is a proposal.

entry.title: Milgram's Obedience Studies
entry.summary: Live debate. The experiments that seemed to show ordinary people would follow orders to hurt strangers. The archives complicate the result.

entry.title: Miguel Never Came Back
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that a character's journey ends in death rather than return. It is an interpretation of a film.

entry.title: Microplastics and Hormones
entry.summary: Live debate. Microplastics are everywhere, including in blood and placentas. Whether they act as endocrine disruptors in people is a question the exposure data cannot yet answer.

entry.title: Microbiome Forensics
entry.summary: Live debate. The bacteria on a body or a phone may identify a person or a place. The research is early.

entry.title: The Michigan Relics
entry.summary: Debunked. Thousands of inscribed objects 'found' in Michigan, said to record ancient migrations. They were made and planted.

entry.title: Mica in the Pyramids
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that mica sheets in Egyptian monuments served an electrical purpose. Mica is present; the electrical use is not.

entry.title: The MH370 Portal Video
entry.summary: Debunked. A video said to show the missing aircraft disappearing into a portal. The video is a composite.

entry.title: The Men in Black
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Men in dark suits who visit witnesses and warn them to keep quiet. The stories are consistent, old, and unsupported by a single verified case.

entry.title: The Memory of Water
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that water retains the properties of substances diluted out of existence. The experiment failed a supervised test.

entry.title: Megalodon in the Trench
entry.summary: Debunked. A giant shark known from teeth, extinct for millions of years, said to survive in the deep ocean. The size of the animal is the argument against it.

entry.title: The Megafauna Extinctions
entry.summary: Live debate. Large animals disappeared from every continent except Africa at the end of the Pleistocene. Climate, humans, or both — and the answer differs by continent.

entry.title: Medusa
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The gorgon's head turns viewers to stone. Explanations have included fossils, masks and ritual, and none is established.

entry.title: Mechanistic Interpretability
entry.summary: Live debate. The attempt to reverse-engineer what a model is computing inside. Results are documented; the general claim is not.

entry.title: MeatSleep
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta told through a series of unsettling videos and posts. It is fiction, and the format is the work.

entry.title: McDonald's Monopoly Rigging
entry.summary: Documented. The promotional game was rigged for years by the man who ran its security, who sold the winning pieces. The FBI investigation is documented.

entry.title: The Maya Tracked Venus
entry.summary: Documented. Maya astronomers recorded the movements of Venus with an accuracy that took European astronomy centuries to match. The tables survive in the Dresden Codex.

entry.title: Maya Blue
entry.summary: Documented. A pigment that survived a thousand years of tropical rain, and whose chemistry was only explained in the twentieth century.

entry.title: The Max Headroom Incident
entry.summary: Documented. Two Chicago television stations were hijacked by a masked figure in 1987. Nobody was ever charged.

entry.title: Match.com's Fake Messages
entry.summary: Documented. A dating service that sent messages from fake accounts to lure users back. The regulator documented it.

entry.title: Mast Cell Activation Syndrome
entry.summary: Live debate. A proposed condition in which mast cells release mediators inappropriately, producing flushing, pain and allergic-type symptoms. The cells are real; the syndrome's criteria are contested.

entry.title: Marvel's Doom Pivot
entry.summary: Documented. Marvel cast Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom after playing Iron Man. The decision is documented; the reasoning is the studio's.

entry.title: The Marshmallow Test
entry.summary: Live debate. Children who waited for a second sweet did better later in life. The correlation replicated weakly, and it is mostly about the family.

entry.title: Markovian Parallax Denigrate
entry.summary: Live debate. Hundreds of Usenet posts in 1996 containing strings of words with no meaning. The posts are archived; their purpose is not known.

entry.title: Mario 3 Is a Stage Play
entry.summary: Documented. A fan theory holds that Super Mario Bros. 3 is staged as a theatre performance — the curtain, the blocks on stands, the card at the end. It is a reading, and the developers have answered it.

entry.title: Marine Ice Cliffs
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that tall ice cliffs at the edge of Antarctica could collapse rapidly, raising sea level faster than models allow. Later work suggests the cliffs are stronger than the hypothesis assumed.

entry.title: Marble Hornets
entry.summary: Fiction. A YouTube series presented as found footage, made by three people, and one of the founding works of the Slender Man mythos.

entry.title: Mantle Plumes
entry.summary: Live debate. Hot rock rising from deep in the mantle is the standard explanation for Hawaii and Iceland. The seismic evidence for the plumes is weaker than the theory requires.

entry.title: The Manna Machine
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A 1978 book argued that the manna of Exodus was produced by a machine the Israelites carried. The argument is built on a medieval mystical text, and there is no machine in the archaeological record.

entry.title: The Mandela Catalogue
entry.summary: Fiction. An analog horror series about 'alternates' replacing people. The name borrows the Mandela effect, and the fiction is explicit.

entry.title: The Man from Taured
entry.summary: Debunked. A traveller at a Japanese airport whose passport was from a country that does not exist. The story has no source, and it is an urban legend.

entry.title: Male Loneliness
entry.summary: Documented. Surveys find that a substantial share of men report no close friends and rely on a partner for emotional support. The pattern is documented; the explanations are contested.

entry.title: Majestic 12
entry.summary: Debunked. A set of documents supposedly signed by Truman, establishing a secret committee on recovered alien craft. The FBI examined them and called them fake, and the forgery is not subtle.

entry.title: The Madden Curse
entry.summary: Debunked. Athletes on the cover of the Madden NFL game are said to be injured the following season. The hit rate is high until you count the seasons that went fine.

entry.title: Lyonesse
entry.summary: Fiction. A sunken kingdom off Cornwall, drowned in a single night, from which Tristan came. It is literature, and the sea floor has been surveyed.

entry.title: Lumon's Board Is Kier
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the mysterious Board in Severance is the company's founder, still directing the firm. It is a reading of the show's theology.

entry.title: The Lost Ten Tribes
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Ten tribes deported by Assyria and never heard from again, and centuries of claims about where they went.

entry.title: The Lost Dutchman Mine
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A German prospector is said to have found a fabulously rich gold mine in the Superstition Mountains and died without revealing it. People have died looking, and nothing has been found.

entry.title: Lost Cosmonauts
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that the Soviet Union lost cosmonauts in orbit and covered it up, based on amateur radio recordings. The archives opened, and the crews are accounted for.

entry.title: The Lost City of Z
entry.summary: Documented. A British explorer vanished looking for a civilisation in the Amazon. The civilisation turned out to be real — but not as a city of stone.

entry.title: The Los Lunas Stone
entry.summary: Debunked. A boulder in New Mexico inscribed with the Ten Commandments in Hebrew, said to be ancient. The inscription is modern.

entry.title: The Longyou Caves
entry.summary: Documented. Twenty-four hand-cut caves in China, with no record of who made them or why. The absence of documentation is the puzzle.

entry.title: The Lonely Runner Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. Runners on a circular track at different constant speeds: each will at some point be far from all the others. It is proved for small numbers of runners and open beyond.

entry.title: Local 58
entry.summary: Fiction. A series of fictional emergency broadcasts, made as analog horror. The format borrows the authority of public information films.

entry.title: The Lobotomy
entry.summary: Documented. Tens of thousands of brains operated on with an ice-pick-like instrument. The rise and fall are both documented.

entry.title: Little Albert
entry.summary: Live debate. A baby conditioned to fear a white rat. The study is famous, the child was never identified, and the ethics were appalling.

entry.title: Linking the Fire
entry.summary: Fiction. The choice at the end of a game about cycles. It is a reading of a fiction, and the fiction is about reading.

entry.title: Linguistic Relativity
entry.summary: Live debate. Does the language you speak shape what you can think? The strong version is dead; the weak version has small, replicated effects that are easy to overstate.

entry.title: Linear A
entry.summary: Documented. The script of Minoan Crete, used for accounting and ritual, and never deciphered. Linear B was cracked because a scholar guessed the language; Linear A has no such handle.

entry.title: Liminal Spaces as the Afterlife
entry.summary: Fiction. An aesthetic of empty corridors, read by some as a glimpse of what comes after. The images are real; the reading is fiction.

entry.title: Light Speed as a Clock Limit
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that the speed of light is not a physical constant but the processing limit of a simulation. The constant is measured; the simulation is an interpretation.

entry.title: Light's Momentum in Matter
entry.summary: Live debate. Does a photon's momentum in a medium follow Minkowski's or Abraham's formula? The argument ran for a century.

entry.title: Life Under the Ice
entry.summary: Live debate. Lakes beneath Antarctica's ice sheet have been sealed for millions of years. Drilling them is a test of whether life persists in isolation.

entry.title: Life on Mars First
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that life appeared on Mars before Earth, and came here on a rock. The mechanism is possible; the evidence is not there.

entry.title: The Library of Alexandria
entry.summary: Documented. The greatest library of the ancient world, and the most over-explained destruction in history. It declined over centuries, and no single fire ended it.

entry.title: Libor Rigging
entry.summary: Documented. Traders manipulated the interest rate that underpinned trillions in loans and derivatives, by submitting figures that suited their books.

entry.title: Ley Lines
entry.summary: Debunked. Straight lines drawn between ancient sites, said to be channels of earth energy. They are drawn after the fact.

entry.title: Legendre's Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. There is always a prime between n² and (n+1)². It has been checked far out and proved nowhere.

entry.title: Why Ten Per Cent Are Left-Handed
entry.summary: Live debate. Hand preference is stable, partly heritable, and not explained. Identical twins disagree about a third of the time, which rules out a simple genetic account.

entry.title: Left Brain, Right Brain
entry.summary: Debunked. The idea that people are logical or creative by hemisphere. The hemispheres do differ, and not like that.

entry.title: Lean Mass Hyper-Responders
entry.summary: Live debate. A subgroup on low-carbohydrate diets shows large rises in LDL cholesterol while remaining lean and metabolically healthy. Whether that is harmless is the question.

entry.title: Leaky Gut
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that increased intestinal permeability allows bacterial products into the blood and drives systemic disease. The permeability is measurable; the disease claims are much larger.

entry.title: Lazar and Element 115
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A man who said he worked on alien craft at Area 51 claimed their fuel was element 115, unknown at the time. Element 115 was synthesised in 2003, and it decays in milliseconds.

entry.title: The Lavon Affair
entry.summary: Documented. Israeli military intelligence recruited Egyptian Jews to bomb Western targets in Egypt, in an attempt to damage relations with the West. The operation was exposed, and the political fallout lasted a decade.

entry.title: The Location of Punt
entry.summary: Live debate. Egypt traded with a land called Punt for a thousand years, and its location has never been fixed. The candidates run from Somalia to Yemen.

entry.title: Lake Nyos
entry.summary: Documented. A crater lake in Cameroon released a cloud of carbon dioxide that killed about 1,700 people overnight. It is the clearest documented case of a limnic eruption.

entry.title: Lake City Quiet Pills
entry.summary: Live debate. A website and a Reddit thread that appeared to be a front for something. The documents are real; the interpretation is not settled.

entry.title: The Labyrinth of Hawara
entry.summary: Documented. A vast mortuary complex described by Herodotus and Strabo, of which only fragments survive.

entry.title: Kumari Kandam
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A lost Tamil landmass said to have sunk south of India, sometimes linked to Lemuria. The ocean floor has been mapped, and there is no continent there.

entry.title: Kubrick Confessed to the Moon Hoax
entry.summary: Debunked. A video appears to show Stanley Kubrick confessing to faking the Moon landings. The video is a hoax, the interview is real and unrelated, and the claim has been circulating since 2015.

entry.title: The Kraken
entry.summary: Live debate. A sea monster described by Norwegian writers, and a possible reference to the giant squid. The animal is real; the identification is inference.

entry.title: Knossos
entry.summary: Documented. The Minoan palace excavated by Arthur Evans, reconstructed in concrete, and argued about ever since.

entry.title: The Klerksdorp Spheres
entry.summary: Debunked. Grooved stone spheres from a South African mine, three billion years old, were said to be manufactured. They are concretions, and the grooves are where crystals grew.

entry.title: Kitty Genovese and the Bystander Effect
