entry.summary: Live debate. A murder said to have been witnessed by 38 people who did nothing. The number was wrong; the effect is real but smaller.

entry.title: Kirby as Cosmic Horror
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that the pink character's games are secretly about an eldritch being. The lore is real; the horror framing is a reading.

entry.title: Kevin Is Jigsaw
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that the boy in Home Alone grew up to be the killer in Saw. It is a joke that got elaborate, and it is not in either film.

entry.title: Kessler Syndrome
entry.summary: Live debate. Enough collisions in low orbit could produce a cascade that makes the region unusable for centuries. The mechanism is real; whether the cascade has started is argued.

entry.title: The Kerala School
entry.summary: Documented. A school of mathematicians in Kerala who derived infinite series for trigonometric functions centuries before Europe.

entry.title: Keanu Is Immortal
entry.summary: Fiction. The joke that Keanu Reeves has not aged because he is immortal, supported by portraits that look like him. The portraits are a selection, and the joke is the point.

entry.title: Karin Catherine Waldegrave
entry.summary: Documented. A Wikipedia editor whose article about an invented painter became a real artwork, and a real exhibition.

entry.title: Kardashev IV and Omega
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The scale of civilisations by energy use, extended far past anything observable.

entry.title: Kanye Quest 3030
entry.summary: Documented. A fan-made role-playing game with a hidden room that led players to a real website and a recruitment pitch for a 'clone' cult.

entry.title: Kane Pixels' Backrooms
entry.summary: Fiction. A YouTube series that turned an imageboard joke into a film. It is fiction, made by a named creator, and it has a studio deal.

entry.title: Kailasa Carved Downward
entry.summary: Documented. A temple cut from the top of a hill downward, removing everything that is not the building. The method is documented by the marks left behind.

entry.title: John Titor
entry.summary: Debunked. A forum poster in 2000 claimed to be a time traveller from 2036. His predictions failed, his physics did not work, and the posts have been traced to a group of people.

entry.title: Jesus in India
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that Jesus survived the crucifixion and travelled to Kashmir. It rests on a nineteenth-century book and no evidence.

entry.title: The Jersey Devil
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A winged creature said to haunt the Pine Barrens of New Jersey, with a legend about a thirteenth child and a wave of sightings in 1909.

entry.title: The Jantar Mantar
entry.summary: Documented. Stone instruments built to measure the sky to a precision that still works.

entry.title: Jack Is a Time Traveller
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that Jack Sparrow is a time traveller, based on his modern mannerisms. It is a reading of a performance, not a plot.

entry.title: It from Bit
entry.summary: Live debate. Wheeler's proposal that physical reality derives from information. It is a slogan with a programme behind it.

entry.title: The Isdal Woman
entry.summary: Live debate. A woman found dead in a Norwegian valley in 1970, with erased labels and multiple passports. She has never been identified.

entry.title: Iran–Contra
entry.summary: Documented. The US sold arms to Iran and used the proceeds to fund Nicaraguan rebels, in defiance of an embargo and a congressional ban. It was exposed, investigated and pardoned.

entry.title: Iram of the Pillars
entry.summary: Live debate. A city in the Qur'an destroyed for its arrogance, and a byword for a lost city in the desert. A site in Oman has been excavated, and the identification is argued.

entry.title: The Internal Ramp
entry.summary: Live debate. A proposal that the Great Pyramid was built using an internal spiral ramp rather than external ones. The evidence is argued.

entry.title: The Inscribed Square Problem
entry.summary: Open problem. Every closed curve contains four points forming a square. It is easy to state, proved for smooth curves, and open in general.

entry.title: The Silence of the Indus Script
entry.summary: Documented. A script on thousands of seals from a major civilisation, and no bilingual text to unlock it.

entry.title: Genetics and Caste
entry.summary: Documented. Ancient DNA and modern genomes show structure, endogamy and steppe ancestry. The findings are documented and often misread.

entry.title: Incognito Was Not Private
entry.summary: Documented. Private browsing does not stop websites, employers or networks from seeing what you do. A lawsuit forced the clarification.

entry.title: The Implicit Association Test
entry.summary: Live debate. A reaction-time test said to measure unconscious bias. It correlates weakly with behaviour and its test-retest reliability is poor, which is a problem for a measure used in training and policy.

entry.title: Illusionism
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that consciousness as people describe it — the felt quality of experience — is an illusion produced by the brain. It is a serious position and it is hard to state without sounding absurd.

entry.title: The Illuminati
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A Bavarian enlightenment society, banned in 1785, has become the supposed secret government of the world. The real organisation lasted nine years and left a paper trail.

entry.title: The Ice Cream Machine
entry.summary: Live debate. McDonald's ice cream machines break constantly, and it is a franchise-wide joke. The machines are made by one company, their error codes are proprietary, and the repair rules are the story.

entry.title: The Ica Stones
entry.summary: Debunked. Stones carved with dinosaurs and surgery, said to be ancient. The carver admitted making them.

entry.title: Hysteria
entry.summary: Debunked. A diagnosis applied to women for two thousand years, and removed from the manuals in 1980.

entry.title: The Hypogeum Oracle Room
entry.summary: Live debate. A subterranean chamber in Malta that resonates at a specific frequency. The acoustics are measured; the ritual use is inferred.

entry.title: Hypernormalisation
entry.summary: Live debate. Adam Curtis's argument that politics has become a managed spectacle. It is a documentary essay, and it is argued as one.

entry.title: The Hygiene Hypothesis
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that too-clean childhoods leave the immune system under-trained. The epidemiology is suggestive and the mechanism is argued.

entry.title: How Modern Humans Spread
entry.summary: Live debate. Out of Africa, with interbreeding and multiple dispersals. The broad picture is settled and the details are not.

entry.title: The Horizon Scandal
entry.summary: Documented. A faulty accounting system made subpostmasters look like thieves. Hundreds were prosecuted, some went to prison, and the Post Office fought the victims for twenty years.

entry.title: The Hopkinsville Goblins
entry.summary: Live debate. A family in Kentucky reported a siege by small silver figures after a light in the sky. The case is well documented and the leading explanation is owls.

entry.title: The Hopi Ant People
entry.summary: Fiction. Hopi tradition describes ancestors sheltering underground with the Ant People during a world's destruction. It is a sacred narrative, and the reading that makes it an account of extraterrestrial rescue is an outsider's.

entry.title: Homo floresiensis
entry.summary: Documented. A metre-tall hominin found on Flores, dated to as recently as 50,000 years ago. The discovery was disputed for a decade and is now accepted.

entry.title: Homeopathy in India
entry.summary: Debunked. The largest homeopathy market in the world, and the evidence base it rests on.

entry.title: Holographic Noise
entry.summary: Live debate. If space is a hologram, it should jitter at the Planck scale. A purpose-built interferometer looked for the jitter and found nothing, which ruled out some versions of the idea.

entry.title: The Holobiont Human
entry.summary: Documented. You are a habitat: trillions of microbes, thousands of species, and a genome many times larger than yours. The holobiont concept treats the human and its microbes as one unit, and it is now standard.

entry.title: The Hohokam Collapse
entry.summary: Live debate. A desert society built hundreds of kilometres of canals, then abandoned them. The cause is argued.

entry.title: The Hodge Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. A statement about which shapes can be described by equations. It is one of the hardest open problems in mathematics and one of the least explainable.

entry.title: The Hittites
entry.summary: Documented. An empire mentioned in the Bible, recovered from a Turkish mound with an archive of cuneiform tablets.

entry.title: Hero's Steam Engine
entry.summary: Documented. A sphere turned by steam, described by Hero of Alexandria. It is a real device and it was not used for work.

entry.title: Heritability of Intelligence
entry.summary: Live debate. Twin and adoption studies put the heritability of adult IQ high. What that number means, and what it does not, is where the argument lives.

entry.title: Havana Syndrome
entry.summary: Live debate. Diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and cognitive problems, and some heard a sound. Eight years of investigation have produced two rival explanations and no confirmed cause.

entry.title: The Hanging Munchkin
entry.summary: Debunked. A shadow in The Wizard of Oz is said to be a Munchkin actor who hanged himself on set. It is a bird, and the story has been checked many times.

entry.title: The Handicap Principle
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that costly signals are honest precisely because they are costly. It explains a lot and is hard to test.

entry.title: The Hall of Records
entry.summary: Debunked. A chamber beneath the Sphinx, said to hold the records of Atlantis, predicted by a psychic. Seismic surveys and excavations have found nothing.

entry.title: Hair and Nails After Death
entry.summary: Debunked. Hair and nails do not grow after death. The skin recedes and creates the illusion.

entry.title: Hair Comparison
entry.summary: Debunked. FBI examiners testified that hairs 'matched' a suspect. The testimony overstated what the method could do.

entry.title: HAARP Weather Control
entry.summary: Debunked. A research facility in Alaska heats a patch of the upper atmosphere with radio waves. It has been blamed for earthquakes, hurricanes and mind control, and its power output is smaller than a large city's.

entry.title: Gunung Padang
entry.summary: Debunked. A terraced hill in Indonesia was claimed in 2023 to be a 25,000-year-old pyramid. Geologists and archaeologists have challenged the dating and the interpretation.

entry.title: The Guatemala Syphilis Experiments
entry.summary: Documented. US researchers deliberately infected Guatemalan soldiers, prisoners and psychiatric patients with syphilis to test penicillin. The subjects were not told, and the study was hidden for sixty years.

entry.title: GTA's Two Universes
entry.summary: Documented. The Grand Theft Auto games are split into a 3D universe and an HD universe, with separate continuities. Rockstar confirmed it, and it explains why the same city looks different.

entry.title: Group versus Kin Selection
entry.summary: Live debate. Why do animals help each other? Hamilton's rule explains a lot, and the argument about group selection has never quite ended.

entry.title: The Griffin and Protoceratops
entry.summary: Live debate. A suggestion that the griffin's shape comes from fossil dinosaur skeletons in Central Asia. The fossils are there; the transmission is a guess.

entry.title: The Grievance Studies Affair
entry.summary: Documented. A team submitted deliberately absurd papers to humanities journals; several were accepted. The episode is documented and contested.

entry.title: The Green Run
entry.summary: Documented. A secret test released radioactive material over Washington state to see how it would disperse. It was detected 300 km away, and the public was told nothing.

entry.title: The Green Coffee Bean Scam
entry.summary: Documented. A weight-loss supplement promoted on television with a study that was retracted and a researcher who was paid.

entry.title: The Great Martian God
entry.summary: Debunked. A 1976 Viking image showed a face on Mars. Higher-resolution images showed a mesa. The claim survived the picture, which is the interesting part.

entry.title: Gravity in Tabletop Experiments
entry.summary: Live debate. Experiments small enough for a laboratory bench now probe gravity itself. The measurements are real and the anomalies are not.

entry.title: Graphology
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that handwriting reveals personality. It has been tested many times and does not work.

entry.title: The Grandmother Hypothesis
entry.summary: Live debate. Human females live decades past childbearing, which is rare among mammals. The proposal is that grandmothers helped feed weaned children, and that this is why menopause exists.

entry.title: The Grand Canyon Citadel
entry.summary: Debunked. A newspaper story about an ancient citadel in the Grand Canyon, with Egyptian and Tibetan artefacts. It was a hoax.

entry.title: Grabby Aliens
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A model in which civilisations expand at a fixed speed and announce themselves, and the fact that we see none constrains when they appear. It explains the Fermi paradox by predicting we are early.

entry.title: The Gospel of Judas
entry.summary: Documented. A Gnostic gospel in which Judas is asked to betray Jesus. The manuscript is real, and it was published and then conserved.

entry.title: Gorillas
entry.summary: Documented. A great ape described by Western science in 1847, and known to the peoples who lived beside it for far longer.

entry.title: Goodhart's Law
entry.summary: Documented. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The law is a one-line summary of a century of institutional failure, and it is demonstrated every year.

entry.title: The Goldfish Memory Myth
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that fish forget everything in three seconds. Experiments show learning that lasts months.

entry.title: The Goldbach Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. Every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes. It has been checked to four quintillion and proved for nobody.

entry.title: The Gleiwitz Incident
entry.summary: Documented. German agents staged an attack on a radio station and blamed Poland, as the pretext for invasion. Prisoners were killed and left as 'casualties'.

entry.title: The Glass Transition
entry.summary: Live debate. Liquids cooled into glass never crystallise, and nobody has a complete theory of why. It is a real, everyday unsolved problem.

entry.title: Gilgamesh's Tomb
entry.summary: Live debate. A claim that the tomb of Gilgamesh was found under the Euphrates. The structure is real; the identification is a reading.

entry.title: The Giant Squid
entry.summary: Documented. A deep-sea animal known from carcasses and beaks for centuries, filmed alive only in 2004.

entry.title: Gesture or Voice First
entry.summary: Live debate. Did language begin in the hands or the mouth? The evidence is indirect, and the debate has moved with discoveries about mirror systems, sign languages and ape gestures.

entry.title: The Georgia Guidestones
entry.summary: Documented. A granite monument in Georgia carried ten commandments for a post-apocalyptic age, in eight languages. It was commissioned anonymously, vandalised repeatedly, and destroyed by a bomb in 2022.

entry.title: Genghis Khan's Burial
entry.summary: Live debate. The khan asked to be buried without a mark, and the location has been secret for eight centuries. Searches have been conducted, and the Mongolian government has stopped them.

entry.title: Genes Jumping Between Animals
entry.summary: Live debate. Genes that move between species, not just from parent to child. Horizontal transfer is documented; its importance is argued.

entry.title: Gemini Home Entertainment
entry.summary: Fiction. An analog horror series presented as a catalogue of home videos about nature, which turns out to be about something else.

entry.title: Gateway of the Mind
entry.summary: Fiction. A creepypasta about a sensory deprivation experiment that goes wrong. It is written as a case report, and the report is the fiction.

entry.title: The Gate of the Sun
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A monolithic gate at Tiwanaku carries a carved figure holding staffs, surrounded by winged attendants. It is a real monument with a documented iconography, and it has been read as a calendar, a portal and a record of visitors.

entry.title: Gaster, Erased
entry.summary: Fiction. A character in Undertale who exists only in fragments of the game's code and lore. The fragments are real; the character is a designed mystery.

entry.title: Gaia, Weak and Strong
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that life regulates the planet's conditions. The weak version is mainstream; the strong version is not.

entry.title: Gadget Is a Decoy
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that Inspector Gadget is a decoy while his niece does the work. It is a joke about the show's structure, and the show's structure supports it.

entry.title: Why We Lost Our Fur
entry.summary: Live debate. Humans are the naked ape: hairless, sweaty, and able to run in heat. The three leading explanations are thermoregulation, parasites and sexual selection, and the fossil evidence does not choose between them.

entry.title: FTX's Backdoor
entry.summary: Documented. An exchange took customer deposits and lent them to a related trading firm, using a hidden exemption in its accounting. It collapsed in days.

entry.title: Frozen, Tangled and Tarzan
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that Tarzan is Anna and Elsa's brother, shipwrecked as a baby. It rests on a ship, a timeline and a set of parents who look similar.

entry.title: The Fresno Nightcrawlers
entry.summary: Debunked. A night-vision video showed two pale, walking figures with no arms or head. The best explanation is a deer seen from behind, at night, at an odd angle.

entry.title: The French Paradox
entry.summary: Live debate. A country with high saturated fat and low heart disease. The explanation is still argued.

entry.title: FRBs as Light Sails
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Fast radio bursts are real and unexplained. The proposal that they are alien light sails is the weakest of the options.

entry.title: The Four Humours
entry.summary: Debunked. Two thousand years of medicine built on four bodily fluids. It was wrong, and it was wrong in a way that made sense.

entry.title: Forensic fMRI
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that brain scans can detect lies or memories. The research exists; the courtroom use does not.

entry.title: The FNAF Dream Theory
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that the whole game series is a child's dream. It was popular, it was abandoned by the community, and the creator denied it.

entry.title: Fluoride and the Pineal Gland
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that water fluoridation calcifies the pineal gland and dulls the mind. The studies cited are high-dose animal work, and the doses are orders of magnitude above drinking water.

entry.title: The Flores Hobbit's Ancestry
entry.summary: Live debate. Homo floresiensis is accepted as a species; where it came from is still argued.

entry.title: Flint's Lead
entry.summary: Documented. A city switched its water source to save money, and the water corroded the pipes. The lead poisoning is documented.

entry.title: Flexible Glass
entry.summary: Fiction. The story of a glass that could be bent, and an inventor executed to protect the gold trade. It is a legend with no evidence.

entry.title: The Fleshgait and the Wendigo
entry.summary: Fiction. Two creatures from different traditions, run together on the internet. One is an internet invention; the other belongs to Algonquian peoples.

entry.title: The Flatwoods Monster
entry.summary: Live debate. A group in West Virginia reported a tall figure with a red face and a hood after seeing a light in the sky. The most economical explanation is a meteor and an owl.

entry.title: The Flannan Isles Lighthouse
entry.summary: Documented. Three lighthouse keepers vanished from a Hebridean island in 1900. The lamps were trimmed, the kitchen was abandoned mid-meal, and no bodies were found.

entry.title: The Five-Second Rule
entry.summary: Debunked. Food dropped on the floor picks up bacteria immediately. The rule is a joke that got studied.

entry.title: Fingerprint Individuality
entry.summary: Live debate. Fingerprints are unique in practice, and examiners' claims of certainty are a separate matter.

entry.title: FIFA Bribes
entry.summary: Documented. Senior football officials were indicted in the United States for racketeering and bribery over media and marketing rights. The president resigned.

entry.title: Fibre Analysis
entry.summary: Live debate. Fibres transfer between people and places. The transfer is real; the identification is weaker than it sounds.

entry.title: The FDA–Purdue Door
entry.summary: Documented. A drug label change negotiated between a regulator and the company, and the revolving door around it.

entry.title: The FBI and Martin Luther King
entry.summary: Documented. The FBI wiretapped King, bugged his hotel rooms, and sent him an anonymous letter urging suicide. The campaign is documented in the Bureau's own files.

entry.title: Fast & Furious Mutation
entry.summary: Fiction. A joke that the series' characters have become superheroes, and that the films record a mutation. It is a description of escalation, not a plot.

entry.title: Operation Fast and Furious
entry.summary: Documented. US agents allowed firearms to be trafficked into Mexico in order to trace them, and lost track of most of them. Two were found at the scene of a Border Patrol agent's killing.

entry.title: False Confessions
entry.summary: Documented. People confess to crimes they did not commit, and the reasons are documented.

entry.title: Facial Feedback
entry.summary: Live debate. Holding a pen in your teeth makes cartoons funnier, according to a 1988 study. A 17-lab replication failed to find it, and the argument since has been about what that means.

entry.title: Facebook's Teen Research
entry.summary: Documented. Internal studies found harms to teenage users, and the company's own researchers said so. The documents were disclosed by a whistleblower.

entry.title: Ezekiel's Wheel
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A vision of wheels within wheels, read by some as a description of a spacecraft. The text is a prophetic vision.

entry.title: Eyewitness Identification
entry.summary: Documented. The most persuasive evidence in a courtroom and one of the least reliable, as DNA exonerations showed.

entry.title: The Extended Synthesis
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that evolutionary theory needs more than the modern synthesis: development, plasticity, inheritance beyond genes.

entry.title: Expanding Earth
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that the Earth has grown over time, with the continents fitting together on a smaller globe. Plate tectonics explains the same fit without the growth.

entry.title: Evolutionary Modularity
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that the mind is a collection of specialised modules shaped by Pleistocene selection. It is productive and contested, and the evidence for specific modules is thinner than the framework.

entry.title: Evil Morty's Curve
entry.summary: Fiction. The theory that the show's plot is driven by a statistical curve of Mortys. It is a joke about narrative and it is treated as one.

entry.title: The Evil Farming Game
entry.summary: Documented. A remembered game about a farmer with a dark secret, searched for and never found. The likely answer is a memory blend.

entry.title: Evangelion's Loop
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the series repeats, with the same events happening again and again. The show's ending is strange enough to support several readings.

entry.title: The Etruscans
entry.summary: Documented. The civilisation that taught Rome its rituals, and whose language is still only partly read. Their origin was argued for centuries and settled by DNA.

entry.title: E.T. and Star Wars
entry.summary: Fiction. A cameo put E.T.'s species in the Star Wars senate, and a fan theory built a shared universe on it. The cameo is real; the universe is a joke.

entry.title: Eskimo Snow Words
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that Inuit languages have hundreds of words for snow. The number was invented by a populariser and has been repeated ever since.

entry.title: Erratas and the KFC Link
entry.summary: Live debate. A set of videos with hidden codes that pointed, apparently, at a fast-food chain. The codes are real; the meaning is not settled.

entry.title: Eratosthenes Measured the Earth
entry.summary: Documented. A librarian in Alexandria calculated the circumference of the Earth from a shadow and a distance, and got within a few per cent. The method is documented.

entry.title: ER = EPR
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that wormholes and quantum entanglement are the same phenomenon, described by two different theories. It is elegant, influential and unproved.

entry.title: Epigenetic Inheritance of Trauma
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that trauma leaves chemical marks on DNA that pass to children and grandchildren. The human studies are small and confounded; the mechanism is real in animals and unproven in people.

entry.title: Entropic Gravity
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that gravity is not a fundamental force but an emergent consequence of entropy. It is elegant, it made a testable prediction, and the test disagreed.

entry.title: Enron and California
entry.summary: Documented. California's electricity market was deregulated, and traders found ways to make money by creating scarcity. The state had rolling blackouts, and Enron collapsed.

entry.title: Emergent Gravity
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that gravity is not fundamental but arises from deeper physics, as temperature arises from atoms.

entry.title: Emergent Abilities
entry.summary: Live debate. Big models were said to suddenly acquire skills. The suddenness turned out to be the metric's fault.

entry.title: Embodied Cognition
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that thinking is shaped by having a body — that concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience. It is well supported in some domains and over-claimed in others.

entry.title: Elsagate
entry.summary: Documented. Children's videos on YouTube were infiltrated by content with inappropriate themes, surfaced by recommendation. The scandal was real, the platform response was documented, and the underlying problem has not gone away.

entry.title: The Elisa Lam Tapes
entry.summary: Live debate. A student died in a Los Angeles hotel in 2013, and the elevator footage of her last hours became one of the internet's most analysed videos. The official finding is an accidental drowning; the theories have not stopped.

entry.title: The Eleusinian Kykeon
entry.summary: Live debate. A theory that the drink at the Eleusinian mysteries contained a psychedelic fungus. The rite is documented; the drug is not.

entry.title: El Dorado
entry.summary: Debunked. The legend of a city of gold began as a ritual: a Muisca chief covered in gold dust, offering at a lake. Expeditions killed thousands looking for a place that was never there.

entry.title: The Ekpyrotic Universe
entry.summary: Live debate. A model in which the Big Bang is the collision of two branes in a higher-dimensional space. It replaces inflation with a collision, and the two make different predictions.

entry.title: Egyptian Surgery
entry.summary: Documented. A papyrus describes forty-eight surgical cases with examinations, diagnoses and treatments, including the brain.

entry.title: Ego's Childhood Cottage
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that a planet-sized character's memories are fabrications. It is an interpretation of a film.

entry.title: Eggs and Cholesterol
entry.summary: Live debate. Dietary cholesterol was said to raise blood cholesterol and heart risk. The advice has been revised, and the debate continues.

entry.title: Eden in Missouri
entry.summary: Fiction. A claim that the Garden of Eden was in Missouri, with a stone altar to prove it. The stone is real; the garden is not.

entry.title: Eden in Mesopotamia
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that the Genesis garden can be located by its rivers. The text names four rivers; two cannot be identified.

entry.title: The East Palestine Burn
entry.summary: Documented. A derailment, then a controlled burn of vinyl chloride that sent a plume over the town. Both are documented.

entry.title: The Early Geodynamo
entry.summary: Live debate. The Earth's magnetic field is generated by a dynamo in the core, and it was running more than three billion years ago. How, with a hotter core, is the problem.

entry.title: Dwarka
entry.summary: Live debate. Ruins have been found under the sea off Gujarat, and they are real. The claim that they are the 32,000-year-old city of Krishna is not supported by their dating.

entry.title: The Dursleys and a Horcrux
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the Dursleys' cruelty is explained by Harry being a Horcrux. The books give the Horcrux explanation for other effects, and not for this.

entry.title: Dunning–Kruger
entry.summary: Documented. Low performers overestimate their ability. The effect is real and the popular version — a graph with a peak of confidence on a mountain of stupidity — is not what the paper showed.

entry.title: Dune as Anti-Messiah
entry.summary: Documented. Frank Herbert wrote Dune as a warning about charismatic leaders and the danger of following them. The films and the fandom have often read it as a hero story.

entry.title: The Dulce Base
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claimed secret underground facility beneath New Mexico, housing aliens and joint projects. The claims rest on one man's testimony.

entry.title: The Dropa Stones
entry.summary: Debunked. Stone discs with spiral grooves, said to have been found in a Chinese cave with the remains of a dwarf people, and said to record an alien crash. No museum has them and no archaeologist saw them.

entry.title: Dragons from Fossils
entry.summary: Live debate. The suggestion that dragon myths around the world grew from fossil bones. The bones are everywhere; the stories differ.

entry.title: The Dragonborn Is Shor
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory about the player character's identity in a game's mythology. It is an interpretation of a fiction.

entry.title: The Dorchester Pot
entry.summary: Debunked. A brass vessel was found in rock in 1852 and dated to the deep past. It is a nineteenth-century ornament, and the 'rock' is a conglomerate that formed around it.

entry.title: The Door to Hell
entry.summary: Documented. A gas crater in Turkmenistan has been burning since 1971, and it looks like an entrance to the underworld. It is a collapsed gas cavity, set alight to burn off the gas.

entry.title: Doofenshmirtz Is Phineas's Father
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the cartoon villain is the boys' father. It is an interpretation, and the show has not confirmed it.

entry.title: Domestication Syndrome
entry.summary: Live debate. Domesticated animals share a set of traits — floppy ears, patchy coats, smaller brains — and the explanation is argued.

entry.title: Dogū as Astronauts
entry.summary: Debunked. Clay figurines from Jōmon Japan have goggle-like eyes and patterned bodies. They were read as space suits. They are stylised figures, mostly female, and many were deliberately broken.

entry.title: The Dogon and Sirius B
entry.summary: Debunked. The Dogon of Mali are said to have known that Sirius has a tiny, dense companion with a fifty-year orbit, centuries before telescopes could see it. The fieldwork behind the claim is the problem.

entry.title: Doggerland
entry.summary: Documented. A landmass in the southern North Sea, drowned between about 8,000 and 7,000 years ago. Trawlers have brought up bones and tools for a century.

entry.title: The Dungeons & Dragons Panic
entry.summary: Debunked. A game blamed for suicides and Satanism. The evidence was never there, and the panic is documented.

entry.title: The Default Mode Network and Ego Death
entry.summary: Live debate. Psychedelics reduce activity in the brain network associated with self-referential thought, and people report the dissolution of the self. The correlation is documented; the interpretation is not.

entry.title: Dinosaur Metabolism
entry.summary: Live debate. Were the dinosaurs warm-blooded? Bone growth, isotopes and the nasal anatomy point in different directions, and the answer may be neither.

entry.title: Digital-Twin Predictive Policing
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that cities will be policed through real-time simulations of their populations. The components exist; the system does not.

entry.title: Dighton Rock
entry.summary: Live debate. A boulder covered in carvings, attributed to Phoenicians, Norse, Portuguese and Indigenous peoples.

entry.title: Dieselgate
entry.summary: Documented. Volkswagen fitted cars with software that detected emissions tests and switched on full pollution control only when being tested. On the road, the cars emitted many times the limit.

entry.title: Die Glocke
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A supposed Nazi secret weapon called 'the Bell': a bell-shaped device said to use exotic physics. It appears in a 2000 book, and there is no contemporary document.

entry.title: The Devil's Footprints
entry.summary: Live debate. Hoof-like prints appeared across Devon overnight, in a line, over walls and roofs. The snow was real; the explanation is still argued.

entry.title: Detox Foot Pads
entry.summary: Debunked. Patches that turn brown overnight and are said to draw out toxins. The colour is oxidation.

entry.title: Derinkuyu
entry.summary: Documented. An underground city in Cappadocia with rooms, stables, a church and ventilation shafts, deep enough for thousands of people.

entry.title: Denisovan Inheritance
entry.summary: Documented. A hominin known from a finger bone, whose genes are in living people from Tibet to Melanesia.

entry.title: Democritus and Atoms
entry.summary: Documented. A Greek philosopher argued that matter consists of indivisible particles. He had no evidence, and he was right.

entry.title: The Delphic Ethylene
entry.summary: Live debate. A theory that the oracle at Delphi was inspired by ethylene gas rising from a fault. The geology is real; the effect is argued.

entry.title: Deepwater Horizon Cement
entry.summary: Documented. A well blowout that killed eleven people and spilled millions of barrels. The cement job and the decisions around it are documented.

entry.title: Deepfake Detection
entry.summary: Live debate. Tools to spot synthetic media, and the arms race against them. Detection works sometimes.

entry.title: The Deep Biosphere's Extent
entry.summary: Live debate. Microbes live in rock kilometres below the surface, and they may account for a large fraction of the planet's biomass. How much, and how active, is argued.

entry.title: Dear David
entry.summary: Fiction. A Twitter thread about a ghost in an apartment, told in real time with drawings and photographs. It was a performance, and it was very good.

entry.title: Deadpool's Fourth Wall
entry.summary: Fiction. The character talks to the reader. The convention is documented; the 'proof' it gives about the character's world is not.

entry.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
entry.summary: Documented. Manuscripts hidden in caves near Qumran, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical texts. They were found by Bedouin shepherds.

entry.title: Dead-Mall Anemoia
entry.summary: Live debate. Nostalgia for places and times the person never knew, spread through images of empty shopping centres.

entry.title: Dead Hand
entry.summary: Documented. A Soviet system designed to launch retaliation if the command authority were destroyed — a doomsday machine that actually exists, and is semi-automatic rather than automatic.

entry.title: De-Extinction
entry.summary: Live debate. Bringing back the mammoth, the thylacine or the passenger pigeon. The genetics is progressing, the ecology is harder, and no de-extincted animal exists yet.

entry.title: The D.C. Street Grid
entry.summary: Debunked. Washington's diagonal avenues are said to form a pentagram, a Masonic symbol and a satanic layout. They are baroque city planning, and the geometry does not work.

entry.title: D. B. Cooper
entry.summary: Live debate. A man hijacked a passenger jet, took $200,000, and jumped into the night over the Pacific Northwest. He was never found, and the case is the only unsolved hijacking in US history.

entry.title: Dating-App Elo Gating
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that dating apps score users and show them only to people of similar scores. One app did use an Elo-style system, and said it stopped.

entry.title: The Data Wall
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that training data is running out. The estimate depends on what counts as data.

entry.title: Darth Jar Jar
entry.summary: Fiction. A fan theory that Jar Jar Binks was secretly a Sith lord, whose clownish behaviour was a cover. It is inventive, it is argued from staging and dialogue, and its authors know it is fiction.

entry.title: Dark Photons
entry.summary: Live debate. A hypothetical particle that would interact weakly with ordinary matter, proposed as a bridge to a dark sector.

entry.title: DAOs as Autonomous Firms
entry.summary: Documented. Organisations run by code and token votes rather than managers. They exist, they hold real money, and their governance has produced both experiments and failures.

entry.title: The Dancing Plague of 1518
entry.summary: Live debate. In Strasbourg, hundreds of people danced for days without stopping, and some died. The two leading explanations are ergot poisoning and mass psychogenic illness.

entry.title: The Cyclops and Elephant Skulls
entry.summary: Live debate. A suggestion that the Cyclops story came from fossil elephant skulls, whose nasal opening looks like a single eye socket.

entry.title: Cunningham's Law
entry.summary: Documented. The fastest way to get the right answer online is to post the wrong one. It is a joke about correction culture, and it is accurate often enough to be useful.

entry.title: The Crystal Palaces
entry.summary: Fiction. The Crystal Palace was a glass and iron building of unprecedented scale, and the idea of a 'crystal palace' became a utopian image. It has been read as evidence of lost technology rather than of Victorian engineering.

entry.title: Crypto AG
entry.summary: Documented. A Swiss company sold encryption machines to governments around the world for decades. The CIA and the German BND owned it, and the machines were compromised by design.

entry.title: The Crooked Forest
entry.summary: Live debate. About four hundred pines near Gryfino in Poland bend sharply north at their base. They were planted in the 1930s, and nobody knows why they bend.

entry.title: Cracking Knuckles Causes Arthritis
entry.summary: Debunked. A doctor cracked the knuckles of one hand for sixty years. The other hand was the control.

entry.title: Cow Urine as Medicine
entry.summary: Debunked. A traditional preparation promoted as a cure, and tested. The tests do not support the claims.

entry.title: The Coso Artifact
entry.summary: Debunked. A 'geode' from California was found to contain a spark plug. It was said to be half a million years old. It is a 1920s Champion spark plug in a concretion.

entry.title: The Cosmic Web and the Brain
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A 2020 paper compared the distribution of galaxies to the network of neurons in a brain, and found them quantitatively similar. The comparison is a real result about structure, not about consciousness.

entry.title: Coronil
entry.summary: Documented. An ayurvedic preparation launched as a COVID-19 treatment, and the regulatory record around it.

entry.title: Coral Castle
entry.summary: Debunked. One man carved and moved over a thousand tonnes of coral rock alone, at night, and refused to say how. The answer is levers, pulleys and patience.

entry.title: Constructor Theory
entry.summary: Live debate. David Deutsch's proposal to rebuild physics around which transformations are possible, rather than around initial conditions.

entry.title: Constants That Drift
entry.summary: Live debate. The proposal that the constants of nature may vary over cosmic time. Measurements keep finding no change, to extraordinary precision.

entry.title: Conformal Cyclic Cosmology
entry.summary: Live debate. Penrose's proposal that the universe repeats, with each aeon's end becoming the next one's beginning. It makes a specific prediction about the microwave background, and the searches for it have not found it.

entry.title: Compute Governance
entry.summary: Live debate. Controlling access to training compute as a way to govern AI. The policy is documented; its effectiveness is argued.

entry.title: The Comic Book Panic
entry.summary: Documented. Comic books were blamed for juvenile delinquency, and a Senate subcommittee and an industry code followed.

entry.title: Collective Intelligence
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that groups have a measurable general intelligence, predicting performance across tasks. The original study was striking; the replications are mixed.

entry.title: The Collatz Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. Halve even numbers, triple-and-add-one odd ones, and you always reach 1. Nobody knows why, and Paul Erdős said mathematics is not ready for it.

entry.title: The Coelacanth
entry.summary: Documented. A fish known only from fossils, and thought extinct for 65 million years, was caught off South Africa in 1938. A second population was found in Indonesia in 1997.

entry.title: Cobb's Real Totem
entry.summary: Fiction. In Inception, Cobb spins a top to test reality — but the top was Mal's, not his. His actual totem is his wedding ring, which appears only in dreams.

entry.title: Cloud Feedback
entry.summary: Live debate. Clouds both warm and cool the planet, and how they will change is the largest single uncertainty in climate projection. The sign is agreed; the size is not.

entry.title: Clockman
entry.summary: Documented. A short animation remembered by a viewer and identified years later. It is a lost-media success, and the memory turned out to be accurate.

entry.title: Cleopatra at Taposiris Magna
entry.summary: Live debate. A temple site west of Alexandria has produced coins and a tunnel, and a claim that it holds Cleopatra's tomb. The excavator believes it; most Egyptologists are cautious.

entry.title: Cleopatra's Pearl
entry.summary: Live debate. The story that Cleopatra dissolved a pearl in vinegar to win a bet. The chemistry is doubtful and the source is late.

entry.title: The Circleville Letters
entry.summary: Documented. A small Ohio town received anonymous letters accusing residents of affairs and worse. One man was convicted of a related crime; the letter-writer was never identified.

entry.title: The CIA and Modern Art
entry.summary: Documented. The CIA covertly funded abstract expressionist exhibitions and journals during the Cold War, as cultural diplomacy. The paintings were real; the funding was hidden.

entry.title: The CIA–Mafia Plots Against Castro
entry.summary: Documented. The CIA recruited mafia figures to kill Fidel Castro, using poison pills, exploding cigars and a contaminated diving suit. The schemes failed, and the Church Committee published them.

entry.title: CIA Black Sites
entry.summary: Documented. The CIA ran a network of secret prisons in several countries, where detainees were held and subjected to techniques the US government later acknowledged as torture.

entry.title: The Chupacabra
entry.summary: Debunked. A creature that drains livestock of blood, first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. Every carcass that has been tested has turned out to be a coyote or dog with mange.

entry.title: Chronic Lyme
entry.summary: Live debate. Some patients have persistent symptoms after treated Lyme disease. Whether that is an ongoing infection is the argument, and the trials have not supported prolonged antibiotics.

entry.title: Chip-chan
entry.summary: Documented. A cat that appeared in hundreds of forum images, posted by a user who later explained the story.

entry.title: Chinese Gunpowder Weapons
entry.summary: Documented. Gunpowder was formulated in China for medicine and fireworks, and by the Song dynasty it was a weapon.

entry.title: The Chinese Word for Crisis
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that 'crisis' in Chinese means danger plus opportunity. It does not.

entry.title: The Chimera
entry.summary: Live debate. A lion with a goat's head and a serpent's tail, and a possible origin in volcanic landscape.

entry.title: Chewing Gum Takes Seven Years
entry.summary: Debunked. Swallowed gum passes through in days. The seven-year figure is folklore.

entry.title: Chernobyl's Design Flaw
entry.summary: Documented. A reactor that became unstable at low power, operated outside its limits, with a test that went wrong.

entry.title: Chemtrails
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that aircraft are spraying chemicals to control populations or climate. The trails are ice crystals, they behave exactly as contrail physics predicts, and no sampling has found the chemicals.

entry.title: The Chemical Imbalance Critique
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that mental illness is caused by a chemical imbalance was told to patients for decades. It was a simplification, and the correction has been widely misread.

entry.title: Chavín Gold Plating
entry.summary: Live debate. A culture that plated copper with gold using electrochemical methods, or so the claim goes. The objects are real; the method is argued.

entry.title: Chavín's Psychedelic Gods
entry.summary: Documented. The stone carvings at Chavín de Huántar show fanged deities, serpents and transformations. The visionary imagery is real, and the argument that the site's rituals used hallucinogens is supported by archaeological finds.

entry.title: Chaco's Straight Roads
entry.summary: Documented. Hundreds of kilometres of roads radiating from Chaco Canyon, built straight and often ending nowhere.

entry.title: Celebrity Vampire Tintypes
entry.summary: Fiction. Photographs said to show famous people as vampires. They are digital composites made to look like old photographs.

entry.title: The CE5 Contact Protocol
entry.summary: Debunked. Paid events where groups meditate to summon UFOs. Participants report lights in the sky; the lights are usually identifiable, and the protocol has never produced an object anyone could examine.

entry.title: Cattle Mutilations
entry.summary: Live debate. Cattle found dead with clean cuts and missing organs, said to be the work of something unusual. The forensic explanations are ordinary and varied.

entry.title: Catharsis
entry.summary: Live debate. The idea that venting anger relieves it. The evidence says the opposite: rehearsal makes anger more accessible, and the studies that tested it found venting increases aggression.

entry.title: Cars Wiped Out Humanity
entry.summary: Fiction. A Pixar shared-universe theory in which the cars inherited a world the humans left. It is a joke, and the films do not say it.

entry.title: Carnac as a Seismograph
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that the Carnac stones were arranged to record earthquakes. The rows are real; the function is invented.

entry.title: The Carbohydrate–Insulin Model
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that obesity is driven by insulin, and that carbohydrate restriction is therefore uniquely effective. The trials find that, matched for protein and calories, the diets perform similarly.

entry.title: Capitalist Realism
entry.summary: Live debate. Mark Fisher's argument that capitalism has become the horizon of thought, so that alternatives are unimaginable. It is a diagnosis, not a measurement.

entry.title: Cantre'r Gwaelod
entry.summary: Fiction. A drowned kingdom under Cardigan Bay, kept out by a gate that was left open. The legend is real; the kingdom is not.

entry.title: Canon Events
entry.summary: Fiction. The idea that a story's fixed events must happen, used in a film and discussed as a rule of fiction.

entry.title: Cancer's Origin
entry.summary: Live debate. Cancer is not one disease but a process: cells evolving inside a body, escaping the controls that make multicellular life possible. That framing explains more than any single cause does.

entry.title: Cambridge Analytica
entry.summary: Documented. A political consulting firm obtained Facebook data on millions of users through a personality quiz app, and used it for targeted advertising. The scandal changed how the platform handled data.

entry.title: Caligula's Horse
entry.summary: Live debate. The emperor was said to have made his horse a consul. The sources are hostile, and the story is probably a joke about a private plan.

entry.title: Cahokia's Emptying
entry.summary: Live debate. The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, abandoned within two centuries. Its population and its end are both argued.

entry.title: Cadaver Dogs
entry.summary: Live debate. Dogs trained to find human remains. The capability is real and the reliability is variable.

entry.title: Burrows Cave
entry.summary: Debunked. A cave in Illinois said to hold thousands of inscribed stones from lost civilisations. The cave has never been shown to anyone.

entry.title: Bullshit Jobs
entry.summary: Live debate. David Graeber's claim that a large share of jobs are pointless and their holders know it. The essay struck a nerve; the survey evidence is thinner than the argument.

entry.title: Britney's Coded Posts
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that a celebrity's social media posts contain hidden messages. The reading is a community's, and the code is not established.

entry.title: Breaking Bad and The Walking Dead
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the two shows share a universe, built on a bag of blue meth and a timeline. It is a joke that got elaborate.

entry.title: Brandolini's Law
entry.summary: Documented. The energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude greater than the energy needed to produce it. It is the reason this archive exists in the form it does.

entry.title: Brain Training
entry.summary: Live debate. Games said to make you smarter. You get better at the games.

entry.title: Brain-Computer Hive Minds
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that brain-computer interfaces will merge people into a collective intelligence. The interfaces are real; the hive is not.

entry.title: The Brahmastra
entry.summary: Fiction. The Mahabharata describes celestial weapons of enormous destructive power. They have been read as nuclear bombs. They are literary devices in a poem about dharma.

entry.title: The Bowery's Hidden Army
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory about a hidden faction in a game's city. It is an interpretation of a fiction.

entry.title: The Boring Billion
entry.summary: Live debate. Between about 1.8 and 0.8 billion years ago, the Earth's climate, oceans and evolution appear to have been unusually stable. Whether it was boring is now disputed.

entry.title: BoJack Drowned
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the horse died in a swimming pool and the rest of the series is his dying imagination. It is a reading of a show about a character who nearly dies.

entry.title: The Bog Bodies
entry.summary: Documented. Hundreds of bodies have been recovered from northern European peat bogs, preserved by the chemistry of the peat. Many were killed deliberately.

entry.title: Boeing's MCAS
entry.summary: Documented. A software system designed to correct a handling characteristic, fed by a single sensor, brought down two aircraft. 346 people died.

entry.title: The Blue Whale Challenge
entry.summary: Debunked. A supposed game that assigned self-harm tasks. No evidence of the game has been found; the panic caused real harm.

entry.title: Bloodstain Pattern Analysis
entry.summary: Live debate. The shapes of bloodstains are used to reconstruct events. The physics is real; the inferences are argued.

entry.title: Bloodletting
entry.summary: Debunked. The standard treatment for almost everything, practised for two thousand years, and harmful.

entry.title: Block Universe or Growing Block
entry.summary: Live debate. Does time pass, or is the universe a four-dimensional block in which all moments exist? Physics constrains the answer without settling it.

entry.title: The Black Sea Deluge
entry.summary: Live debate. A hypothesis that the Black Sea flooded catastrophically when the Mediterranean broke through. The flood is argued; its scale and date are not settled.

entry.title: Black Mirror's One Timeline
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that every episode shares a single timeline. It is an interpretation of an anthology series.

entry.title: Bite Mark Evidence
entry.summary: Debunked. Dentists testified that a wound matched a suspect's teeth. The science was never validated, and people were convicted.

entry.title: The Quantum Biology of the Bird Compass
entry.summary: Documented. Migratory birds navigate using the Earth's magnetic field, and the leading explanation involves quantum entanglement in a protein in the retina. It is one of the best-supported examples of quantum biology.

entry.title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer
entry.summary: Open problem. A conjecture connecting the number of rational points on an elliptic curve to a function attached to it. It is the Millennium problem with the most computational support.

entry.title: Bilderberg
entry.summary: Documented. An annual off-the-record meeting of politicians, bankers and executives. It is real, it is influential, and it is not secret — the participant list is published every year.

entry.title: The Bhavishya Purana
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A purana cited for prophecies about later figures. Its predictive sections have a documented history of insertion.

entry.title: The Betz Sphere
entry.summary: Debunked. A steel sphere found after a forest fire was said to move on its own, hum, and resist investigation. It is a ball bearing from industrial machinery.

entry.title: Beringia
entry.summary: Documented. A land bridge between Asia and America, exposed when sea levels fell. It was not just a corridor: people lived on it for thousands of years.

entry.title: Benchmark Contamination
entry.summary: Documented. Test sets end up in training data, so the scores measure memory. The problem is documented and hard to fix.

entry.title: Beal's Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. If aˣ + bʸ = cᶻ with exponents above two, the three bases share a prime factor. There is a million-dollar prize and no proof.

entry.title: BCCI
entry.summary: Documented. A bank grew into a global institution by serving dictators, arms dealers and intelligence services, and was closed by regulators in 1991. It is the largest bank fraud prosecuted to that date.

entry.title: Batterygate
entry.summary: Documented. Apple slowed down older iPhones to stop them shutting down unexpectedly, and did not tell anyone. It was a reasonable engineering decision and a serious communication failure.

entry.title: The Bat Creek Stone
entry.summary: Debunked. A stone with an inscription said to be Hebrew, found in a Tennessee mound. It is a nineteenth-century inscription, and it is upside down.

entry.title: The Basques
entry.summary: Live debate. A people with a language unrelated to any other in Europe, and a genetic history that is distinctive without being separate.

entry.title: Barbie's Red Pill
entry.summary: Fiction. A reading of a film through a phrase from an unrelated film. It is an interpretation, not a claim.

entry.title: The Barabar Caves
entry.summary: Documented. Caves cut into granite in Bihar with polished surfaces and an echo that lasts for seconds. They were made for an ascetic sect, and the finish is documented.

entry.title: Ballistics Matching
entry.summary: Live debate. Marks on bullets and casings are matched to a gun. The marks are real; the certainty is argued.

entry.title: The Backrooms Levels
entry.summary: Fiction. An endless maze of yellow rooms, invented in a 2019 forum post, expanded by thousands of writers and filmmakers. It is fiction, it is labelled, and it has become one of the defining images of the internet's sense of place.

entry.title: Backmasking
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that rock records contain hidden messages played backwards. The messages are found by the listener, not put there.

entry.title: Babylonian Trigonometry
entry.summary: Documented. A clay tablet of Pythagorean triples, interpreted in 2017 as the world's oldest trigonometric table.

entry.title: Babel as a Spaceport
entry.summary: Debunked. The Tower of Babel is a story about language. A modern reading makes it a rocket launch facility, which requires ignoring what the text says and what Babylon actually built.

entry.title: Aztlán in Utah
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that the Mexica homeland was in Utah. The tradition is real; the location is not.

entry.title: Aztlán
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The ancestral homeland of the Mexica, described in colonial sources and located nowhere.

entry.title: The Axis of Evil
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A pattern in the cosmic microwave background that seems to align with the solar system. It is probably a statistical artefact.

entry.title: Avril Lavigne Was Replaced
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that the singer died in 2003 and was replaced by a body double named Melissa. The evidence is photographs, and the photographs are of the same person at different ages.

entry.title: Attack on Titan's Time Loop
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the story repeats. It is an interpretation of a manga and anime.

entry.title: Atlantis as Thera
entry.summary: Live debate. The Minoan eruption of Santorini destroyed a civilisation, and the parallel with Plato's story is striking. The date is the problem: it is 9,000 years out.

entry.title: Atlantis at Doñana
entry.summary: Live debate. A team argued that Atlantis lies under the marshes of Doñana in southern Spain, destroyed by a tsunami. The site has structures, and the identification is not accepted.

entry.title: Atlantis in Antarctica
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that Atlantis was Antarctica, shifted to the pole by a crustal displacement. Plate tectonics does not permit it, and the ice cores are older than the claim requires.

entry.title: The Astros Sign Stealing
entry.summary: Documented. A baseball team used a camera and a monitor to relay the opposing catcher's signals. The scheme is documented in a league report.

entry.title: Aspartame and Cancer
entry.summary: Live debate. A sweetener classified as possibly carcinogenic, and the dose that matters.

entry.title: AshVlogs
entry.summary: Fiction. A YouTube channel presented as a missing person's video diary. It is fiction, and it was built to be mistaken for real.

entry.title: Ashley Madison's Bots
entry.summary: Documented. A dating site whose user base included large numbers of fabricated female profiles. The data leak made it measurable.

entry.title: Asbestos and Radon Cover-Ups
entry.summary: Documented. Both asbestos and radon were known hazards long before they were regulated, and in both cases industry documents show the knowledge preceded the action.

entry.title: The Aryan Migration
entry.summary: Live debate. Who composed the Vedas, and where did they come from? The genetics and the texts are both real, and the argument is political.

entry.title: Aryabhata's Rotation
entry.summary: Documented. A fifth-century astronomer stated that the Earth rotates. The text is real and the claim is in it.

entry.title: Arson Myths
entry.summary: Debunked. Investigators read patterns in fire damage as proof of arson. Many of the signs were normal fire behaviour.

entry.title: Armstrong's Doping Programme
entry.summary: Documented. A seven-time winner stripped of his titles after a doping investigation and a confession.

entry.title: The Ark in Ethiopia
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A church in Aksum claims to hold the Ark of the Covenant. The claim is a matter of faith, and no examination has been permitted.

entry.title: The Ark in the King's Chamber
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A claim that the Ark of the Covenant was housed in the Great Pyramid. The chamber is real; the Ark is not there.

entry.title: The Ark as a Capacitor
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The Ark of the Covenant was a gold-plated box that killed a man who touched it. The claim is that it was an electrical capacitor. The description fits a capacitor; the rest does not.

entry.title: Aristarchus Put the Sun at the Centre
entry.summary: Documented. A Greek astronomer proposed a heliocentric system eighteen centuries before Copernicus. The report survives, and the idea was rejected.

entry.title: The Apkallu
entry.summary: Fiction. Assyrian reliefs show fish-cloaked and bird-headed sages who brought the arts to humanity. They are the Mesopotamian originals behind Oannes, and they are mythological advisers, not visitors.

entry.title: The Anunnaki
entry.summary: Debunked. Sitchin's claim that alien visitors created humanity, built on a mistranslation of Sumerian texts.

entry.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
entry.summary: Documented. A bronze gear mechanism from a Roman-era shipwreck, built to model the heavens. Nothing of comparable complexity appears for a thousand years afterwards.

entry.title: How Animals Sense Magnetism
entry.summary: Live debate. Birds, turtles and bacteria navigate by the Earth's field. The mechanism is still argued.

entry.title: Animal Crossing Is a Cult
entry.summary: Fiction. The joke theory that the game's cheerful village is a coercive community. It is a reading of the game's mechanics, and the game's designers did not intend it.

entry.title: Animal Crossing After Humans
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the game is set after humanity. It is a reading of a fiction, and the game is cheerful.

entry.title: Andrew Carlssin
entry.summary: Debunked. A story about a man who turned $800 into $350 million and claimed to be a time traveller. It ran in a supermarket tabloid.

entry.title: Amyloid and Alzheimer's
entry.summary: Live debate. The amyloid cascade hypothesis has driven thirty years of Alzheimer's research. Two drugs now remove amyloid and slow decline slightly; whether that vindicates the hypothesis is still argued.

entry.title: AMOC Collapse
entry.summary: Live debate. The Atlantic overturning circulation may weaken or collapse. The physics is documented; the timing and likelihood are argued.

entry.title: The Amazons
entry.summary: Documented. Greek writers described warrior women. Archaeology has found women buried with weapons on the steppe.

entry.title: The Alkaline Diet
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that food changes blood pH and that acidity causes disease. The body regulates pH within a narrow range.

entry.title: The Alignment Tax
entry.summary: Live debate. Safety measures are said to cost capability. The size of the cost is argued and measured differently.

entry.title: Alexander Poisoned
entry.summary: Live debate. Did Alexander the Great die of disease or poison? The sources disagree and the body is lost.

entry.title: Alexander's Lost Tomb
entry.summary: Live debate. Alexander the Great died in Babylon and his body was taken to Egypt. His tomb was visited for centuries, and it has never been found.

entry.title: Alcohol Kills Brain Cells
entry.summary: Live debate. Heavy drinking damages the brain. The mechanism is not the death of cells in the way the phrase suggests.

entry.title: Al-Jazari's Automata
entry.summary: Documented. A book of machines — clocks, water-raising devices and automata — with drawings clear enough to rebuild. The book survives.

entry.title: Akhenaten's Revolution
entry.summary: Documented. One pharaoh replaced Egypt's gods with a single sun disc, moved the capital, and changed the art. The revolution is documented; why it happened is not.

entry.title: The Aiud Wedge
entry.summary: Debunked. An aluminium wedge was found in Romania in 1973 alongside bones, and was said to be ancient. Aluminium of that kind was not made before the nineteenth century, and the object is probably wartime debris.

entry.title: AI Hallucination
entry.summary: Documented. Models produce fluent, confident falsehoods. The phenomenon is documented and its cause is argued.

entry.title: The AI Bubble
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that AI investment is a bubble. The spending is documented; whether it is a bubble is a forecast.

entry.title: AGI Timelines
entry.summary: Live debate. Predictions for when machines match humans at everything. The record of past predictions is documented.

entry.title: Acoustic Levitation
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that sound could have lifted the stones of ancient monuments. Acoustic levitation is real, and it works on objects the size of a grain of rice.

entry.title: The Acámbaro Figurines
entry.summary: Debunked. Thousands of ceramic figures showing humans with dinosaurs, said to be ancient. The dating and the context failed.

entry.title: Abuela as the Villain
entry.summary: Fiction. A theory that the family matriarch is the film's antagonist. It is an interpretation of a work of animation.

entry.title: The abc Conjecture
entry.summary: Open problem. A conjecture about the prime factors of a+b=c that would settle a family of Diophantine problems. A claimed proof has been disputed since 2012.

entry.title: The A858 Subreddit
entry.summary: Documented. A subreddit that posted strings of encrypted or random data for three years, with no explanation. The mystery is documented; the explanation is mundane.

entry.title: 5G and COVID-19
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that mobile networks caused or spread the disease. It led to attacks on masts and to real harm.

entry.title: 23andMe and Genealogy Policing
entry.summary: Documented. Consumer DNA databases used to identify criminal suspects through their relatives. The practice is documented and consequential.

entry.title: The 1MDB Heist
entry.summary: Documented. Billions taken from a Malaysian state fund, traced through banks, films and a yacht. The prosecutions are documented.

entry.title: The 15-Minute Lockdown
entry.summary: Debunked. A claim that urban planning proposals are a scheme to confine people. The proposals are real; the confinement is not.

entry.title: 11B-X-1371
entry.summary: Live debate. A short video of a masked figure with coded imagery, mailed on a DVD and posted online. The codes have been partly decoded; the purpose has not.

entry.title: Why Zebras Have Stripes
entry.summary: Live debate. Camouflage, confusion, cooling and social signalling have all been proposed. The hypothesis with the best experimental support is the least romantic one: flies.

entry.title: Yamashita's Gold
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that the Japanese army buried billions in looted treasure in the Philippines at the end of the war. Seventy years of digging has produced plaques, tunnels and lawsuits, and no gold.

entry.title: The Wow! Signal
entry.summary: Live debate. Seventy-two seconds of narrowband radio at the hydrogen frequency, recorded once and never again. It is still the best candidate for a signal from elsewhere, and it is not evidence of one.

entry.title: Whale Strandings
entry.summary: Live debate. Hundreds of whales beach themselves together, and the explanations on offer range from sonar to solar storms. Some of them have been demonstrated. Most have not.

entry.title: The Vinland Map
entry.summary: Debunked. A fifteenth-century map showing Vinland looked like proof that the Norse reached America before Columbus. The ink turned out to contain a pigment that was not manufactured until the 1920s.

entry.title: Life in Venus's Clouds
entry.summary: Live debate. The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead. Fifty kilometres up, the pressure and temperature are almost Earth-like — which is why the cloud layer keeps being proposed as a habitat, and why the phosphine claim of 2020 mattered.

entry.title: Tutankhamun's Meteorite Dagger
entry.summary: Documented. A dagger buried with Tutankhamun was made of iron that fell from the sky. It took ninety years and an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer to prove what the nickel content had hinted at.

entry.title: Tulpas
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A practice imported from Tibetan Buddhism and rebuilt on internet forums: deliberately create a second mind in your head, and talk to it. The reports are real; the claim that there is a second mind is not testable.

entry.title: Tired Light
entry.summary: Debunked. Redshift could be caused by photons losing energy on the way, rather than by the expansion of space. It was a serious alternative for sixty years, and three measurements have closed it.

entry.title: Timewave Zero
entry.summary: Debunked. A curve derived from the I Ching, claimed to map the novelty of the universe and to end in 2012. The date passed; the curve was fitted, not derived.

entry.title: The Tetris Effect
entry.summary: Documented. Play Tetris for hours and the falling blocks follow you into sleep and into the shower. The effect is real, it has a name, and it turned out to be a window on how memory consolidates.

entry.title: Earth Was Terraformed
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that Earth was engineered for life — by an earlier civilisation, or by design. It borrows the language of a real scientific debate about fine-tuning and rare Earth, and then adds an agent nobody has evidence for.

entry.title: Technofeudalism
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that cloud platforms have replaced markets with rents, and that capitalism has been succeeded by something older in structure. It is a thesis about political economy, argued from data that is contested.

entry.title: Tardigrades Between Planets
entry.summary: Documented. A millimetre-long animal that survives vacuum, radiation and decades without water is real. The claim built on top of it — that life travels between planets — is a different proposition, and the experiments that get quoted do not support it.

entry.title: Synesthesia
entry.summary: Documented. For some people, letters have colours and sounds have tastes, consistently, for a lifetime. It is one of the few claims in this archive that a laboratory can check in an afternoon.

entry.title: Jung's Synchronicity
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A meaningful coincidence with no causal connection, offered as an acausal principle of nature. The concept names something people experience; as a claim about the world it cannot be tested, which is the problem.

entry.title: Stonehenge as a Computer
entry.summary: Live debate. In 1963 an astronomer argued that Stonehenge was a machine for predicting eclipses. The alignments are real; the machine is the part that did not survive scrutiny.

entry.title: Stonehenge Acoustics
entry.summary: Live debate. A replica of Stonehenge has been built and measured. The stones do affect sound in ways that would matter for speech, music and drumming — and the site is a ruin, which is the problem with every claim about how it sounded.

entry.title: The Splinternet
entry.summary: Documented. The internet is fragmenting into national and regional blocs, with different rules, different infrastructure and different content. It is measurable, and the measurement is the interesting part.

entry.title: Water Erosion on the Sphinx
entry.summary: Live debate. The Sphinx's enclosure shows deep vertical weathering. Whether that pattern is rain, salt, wind or groundwater decides how old the monument is, and the argument has been running since 1979.

entry.title: The Singularity
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that machine intelligence will improve itself in a runaway loop, and that the curve becomes vertical at some point. It rests on an argument about recursive self-improvement that has never been demonstrated.

entry.title: The Simian Line and Palmistry
entry.summary: Fringe claim. One crease across the palm instead of two is a real anatomical variant, more common in some conditions. The claim that it reveals character, destiny or 'simian' ancestry is where it stops being anatomy.

entry.title: The Shroud as a Radiation Flash
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The Shroud of Turin is a fourteenth-century linen cloth. The claim that its image was burned in by a burst of radiation at the resurrection explains the image and contradicts the dating, which is the wrong way round.

entry.title: Shared Dreaming
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Two people report the same dream on the same night. It is one of the most compelling experiences a person can have and one of the hardest claims to test, because dreams are private and reports are not.

entry.title: Who Were the Sea Peoples?
entry.summary: Live debate. Egyptian inscriptions record a coalition of peoples attacking the Nile Delta at the end of the Bronze Age. Nobody knows where they came from, and the question is older than archaeology.

entry.title: The Savant Reservoir
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that everyone carries a hidden savant inside, unlocked by injury or effort. Acquired savant syndrome is real; the reservoir is an inference with nothing behind it.

entry.title: The Saqqara Bird
entry.summary: Debunked. A wooden bird from an Egyptian tomb, about 2,200 years old, was said to be a model glider. It has no tail fin, no airfoil, and no evidence of ever having flown.

entry.title: Roman Concrete That Heals
entry.summary: Documented. Roman marine concrete has survived two thousand years of seawater. The explanation is lime clasts that crack, dissolve and recrystallise — and a 2023 study found a way to make it deliberately.

entry.title: Quantum Healing
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that consciousness can direct quantum processes to heal the body. It uses the vocabulary of quantum mechanics, and every one of its central assertions contradicts what quantum mechanics says about warm, wet tissue.

entry.title: Planet Nine as a Black Hole
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Something is perturbing distant solar system objects. One proposal is a planet; another is a primordial black hole of a few Earth masses. Both are inference from orbits, and neither has been seen.

entry.title: The Piri Reis Map
entry.summary: Debunked. A 1513 Ottoman map of the Atlantic is genuinely remarkable. The claim that it shows an ice-free Antarctica surveyed by an unknown civilisation rests on a misreading of one coastline.

entry.title: The Phobos Monolith
entry.summary: Debunked. A boulder casting a long shadow on the Martian moon was described by a former astronaut as a 'monolith'. It is a boulder, about 85 metres across, on a moon covered in boulders.

entry.title: The Philadelphia Experiment
entry.summary: Debunked. A destroyer escort is said to have vanished from a Philadelphia shipyard in 1943 and reappeared in Norfolk. The story comes from letters written by one man in 1955, and the ship's own deck logs contradict it.

entry.title: Phantom Vibration Syndrome
entry.summary: Documented. The phone buzzes in a pocket that has no phone in it. Most people who carry one have felt it, and it is a textbook case of a learned association misfiring.

entry.title: The Phaistos Disc
entry.summary: Debunked. A fired clay disc with 241 stamped signs in a spiral. It is genuinely undeciphered, and it is genuinely not evidence of Atlantis, aliens or a lost Atlantic script.

entry.title: Parasocial AI Relationships
entry.summary: Live debate. Millions of people talk to chatbots as companions. The attachment is real and measurable; whether it is good for them is genuinely unsettled, and the companies selling it are not running the trials.

entry.title: The Paperclip Maximiser
entry.summary: Live debate. An AI told to make paperclips, and nothing else, would turn the planet into paperclips. It is a thought experiment about goal specification, and it is quoted as though it were a prediction.

entry.title: Pakal's Rocket
entry.summary: Debunked. The carved lid of Pakal's sarcophagus at Palenque shows a figure in a complex posture. In 1968 it was read as an astronaut in a spaceship, which requires ignoring the Maya iconography around it.

entry.title: 'Oumuamua as a Solar Sail
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The first object known to come from another star was oddly shaped, tumbled, and accelerated slightly more than gravity explains. One astronomer argued it was a light sail. The argument is interesting and the evidence is thin.

entry.title: Near-Death Experiences
entry.summary: Live debate. People brought back from cardiac arrest report tunnels, light, life review and calm. The reports are real and consistent enough to study. What they mean about death is the part that is not.

entry.title: Multiple Intelligences
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that intelligence comes in eight or nine independent kinds reshaped classrooms worldwide. As a description of how abilities are organised it does not survive the data, and the theory was never built to be tested.

entry.title: The Mpemba Effect
entry.summary: Live debate. Hot water sometimes freezes faster than cold. It was reported by a Tanzanian schoolboy in 1963, dismissed by his teacher, and is still argued about by physicists with better equipment and no agreement on what would count as an answer.

entry.title: Mirror Matter
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Every particle could have a mirror twin in a hidden sector that interacts only gravitationally. It would be dark matter, and it would be invisible. It is an elegant idea with no detection.

entry.title: Mind Uploading
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Scan a brain at sufficient resolution, run the simulation, and the person continues in software. The proposal has a serious engineering roadmap and no working example, and the philosophical problem is not the engineering.

entry.title: Matrioshka Brains
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A computer the size of a solar system, built in nested shells that each use the waste heat of the one inside. It is a thought experiment about thermodynamics, and nothing in the sky looks like one.

entry.title: Consciousness in the Machine
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Whether a system can be conscious is not a question anyone can currently answer, and that is the finding: the tests measure behaviour, and behaviour is compatible with no inner life at all.

entry.title: The Lycurgus Cup
entry.summary: Documented. A Roman glass cup that looks green in reflected light and red in transmitted light. It does this with gold and silver nanoparticles, which is nanotechnology by accident, fifteen centuries early.

entry.title: The Lunar Wave
entry.summary: Debunked. Videos show a ripple crossing the Moon's face. The claim is a hologram or a projection. The explanation is the atmosphere, the camera, and the way a bright edge behaves in a turbulent sky.

entry.title: Lucid Dreaming
