entry.summary: Documented. People can know they are dreaming while asleep, and say so from inside the dream. That was verified with eye movements in 1980, which makes it one of the few dream claims with a laboratory receipt.

entry.title: Loop Quantum Gravity
entry.summary: Live debate. A theory in which space itself is quantised into a network of finite loops. It is mathematically developed, predicts almost nothing measurable, and is one of the two main attempts at quantum gravity.

entry.title: The London Hammer
entry.summary: Debunked. A hammer found encased in rock, said to be 400 million years old. The rock is a concretion that formed around a nineteenth-century tool, which is what the tool is.

entry.title: Nessie as a Giant Eel
entry.summary: Live debate. Environmental DNA sampling of Loch Ness found eel DNA in most samples and no reptilian DNA at all. The eel hypothesis is the most parsimonious one on offer, which is not the same as evidence for a giant eel.

entry.title: The Liar's Dividend
entry.summary: Documented. Deepfakes do not need to fool anyone to do damage. Their existence lets the guilty deny real evidence as fake — and the studies find that it works.

entry.title: The Kensington Runestone
entry.summary: Debunked. A Minnesota farmer found a stone in 1898 claiming a Norse expedition reached the American interior in 1362. Runologists have been unanimous for a century that the inscription is nineteenth-century Swedish.

entry.title: The Kardashev Scale
entry.summary: Documented. A three-step classification of civilisations by energy use, invented for a Soviet radio astronomy paper. It measures nothing we can observe, and it is used constantly as though it did.

entry.title: The Iron Pillar of Delhi
entry.summary: Documented. A six-tonne iron pillar from the Gupta period that has barely rusted in 1,600 years. It is not a lost technology; it is phosphorus, and a dry climate.

entry.title: The Interface Theory of Perception
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that perception is a desktop interface, useful but not true, and that evolution optimises for fitness rather than accuracy. It is a serious argument in the philosophy of perception with an empirical claim that has been contested.

entry.title: The Inner Core's Spin
entry.summary: Live debate. The solid iron ball at the centre of the planet may rotate slightly differently from the rest of it. The claim rests on subtle differences between earthquake waves recorded decades apart, and the disagreement is about the data as much as the physics.

entry.title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
entry.summary: Documented. Encrypted traffic is being recorded today so it can be read when quantum computers are able to break the encryption. It is not a theory about the future; it is guidance from the agencies, and a migration that is already under way.

entry.title: Grey Goo
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Self-replicating nanobots that consume the biosphere. It comes from a 1986 book about molecular manufacturing, and the physics of building it has never been demonstrated.

entry.title: The Green Children of Woolpit
entry.summary: Live debate. Two children with green skin and an unknown language appeared in a Suffolk village in the twelfth century. The story is in two chronicles, and the explanations on offer are all more ordinary than the story.

entry.title: Greek Fire
entry.summary: Live debate. A Byzantine incendiary that burned on water and was projected from ships. The recipe was a state secret, and it was kept: nobody knows exactly what it was.

entry.title: The Great Oxidation Event
entry.summary: Documented. About 2.4 billion years ago the atmosphere filled with oxygen, the planet froze, and most of the life then living died. The evidence is in rocks that record the moment the air changed.

entry.title: The Great Attractor
entry.summary: Documented. Galaxies across a wide region flow toward something in the direction of Centaurus, and for two decades nobody could see what. The answer turned out to be larger than the thing they were looking for.

entry.title: The Grail Bloodline
entry.summary: Debunked. The claim that the Holy Grail is not a cup but a bloodline, descending from Jesus, and that a secret society has guarded it. The society was invented in 1956, and its documents were forgeries.

entry.title: The Google Effect
entry.summary: Documented. People remember where to find information rather than the information itself. The 2011 paper that named it is famous; the replications are mixed, which is the honest state of the finding.

entry.title: The Global Consciousness Project
entry.summary: Debunked. A network of random number generators, said to deviate from randomness when large numbers of people are emotionally engaged. The statistics do not survive the way the events were chosen.

entry.title: The Giza Power Plant
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The claim that the Great Pyramid was a machine for generating electricity, with the King's Chamber as a resonant cavity. It is an engineering hypothesis with no artefact of any machine in it.

entry.title: The Giraffe's Neck
entry.summary: Live debate. Lamarck's favourite example is not a Lamarckian one. The neck has seven vertebrae, like yours, and the best explanation is not that giraffes stretched.

entry.title: Geopolymer Pyramids
entry.summary: Live debate. A French chemist proposed that the pyramid's blocks were cast from a limestone geopolymer rather than quarried. The idea explains some odd features and is contradicted by others, and the argument has been running for forty years.

entry.title: The Gateway Process
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A 1983 CIA report describes consciousness as a hologram and out-of-body travel as a change in brainwave frequency. It is a literature review written by one officer, and it is cited as though it were a finding.

entry.title: The Ganzfeld Effect
entry.summary: Documented. Put half ping-pong balls over someone's eyes, play white noise, and within minutes most people start to hallucinate. The effect is real; the parapsychology built on top of it is not.

entry.title: Folie à Deux
entry.summary: Documented. A delusion shared by two people in a close relationship, usually one dominant and one suggestible. It is rare, it is real, and the modern diagnostic manuals have quietly stopped calling it a separate illness.

entry.title: The Flynn Effect
entry.summary: Documented. Measured intelligence rose by about three points a decade through the twentieth century, in every country with good data. Then, in several of them, it stopped. Both halves of that sentence are strange.

entry.title: The Feejee Mermaid
entry.summary: Debunked. A mermaid exhibited by P. T. Barnum was a monkey's torso sewn to a fish's tail. It made money, started a genre, and is still in a museum drawer with the stitching visible.

entry.title: The Face on Mars
entry.summary: Debunked. A mesa in the Cydonia region looked like a face at Viking resolution. Higher-resolution images, taken twenty-two years later, show a mesa. The interesting part is why the first image looked the way it did.

entry.title: Europa's Ocean
entry.summary: Live debate. Beneath fifteen kilometres of ice, Europa has more liquid water than all of Earth's oceans. Whether anything lives in it is unknown, and a spacecraft is on its way to look.

entry.title: Earthquake Prediction
entry.summary: Live debate. Nobody can say where and when a large earthquake will happen. A great deal of money and a long list of methods have gone into trying, and the failures are more instructive than the successes.

entry.title: Dyson Spheres
entry.summary: Live debate. A civilisation that captured all its star's light would be visible from far away, as an excess of infrared and a deficit of visible light. Astronomers have looked, and found candidates that turned out to be dust.

entry.title: The Dendera Light
entry.summary: Debunked. A relief at Dendera shows a bulb-shaped object with a snake inside it. The claim that it depicts an electric lamp ignores the rest of the scene, which explains it.

entry.title: Déjà Vu
entry.summary: Live debate. The feeling that this has happened before, with no memory of when. Most people have it, nobody has a settled explanation, and the one thing it is not is evidence of a previous life.

entry.title: Déjà Rêvé
entry.summary: Live debate. The sense that this moment was dreamed before. It is distinct from déjà vu, it is common, and the tempting explanation — that the dream predicted the event — is the one the evidence does not support.

entry.title: Dark Flow
entry.summary: Live debate. A 2008 analysis reported that galaxy clusters are all drifting toward a patch of sky beyond the observable universe. If true it would break the assumption that the universe looks the same in every direction. Later data did not confirm it.

entry.title: Damascus Steel
entry.summary: Live debate. Blades with a watery pattern, made from crucible steel imported from India, and famous for sharpness. The technique was lost in the eighteenth century, and the nanoscale explanation is contested.

entry.title: The Crystal Skulls
entry.summary: Debunked. A dozen quartz skulls were said to be pre-Columbian, and one was said to be the work of aliens or Atlanteans. Microscopy found nineteenth-century lapidary tools on every one that has been examined.

entry.title: The Cottingley Fairies
entry.summary: Debunked. Two girls photographed fairies in a Yorkshire garden, and Sherlock Holmes's creator believed them. Sixty years later they admitted the fairies were paper cut-outs pinned to a bush.

entry.title: Cosmic Censorship
entry.summary: Live debate. General relativity allows singularities with no event horizon — naked points where physics stops and the universe can be seen to break. Penrose conjectured they cannot form. Nobody has proved it.

entry.title: The Copper Scroll
entry.summary: Live debate. One Dead Sea Scroll is not a text but a treasure map: sixty-four locations, quantities of gold and silver, and no treasure ever found. It is the only scroll in the collection that reads like an inventory.

entry.title: Collective Effervescence
entry.summary: Documented. Durkheim's term for what happens when a crowd assembles and feels something together. It is not mysticism; it is the mechanism by which rituals make beliefs feel true.

entry.title: Chronostasis
entry.summary: Documented. Glance at a clock and the first second seems to last longer. The clock is fine; your brain is filling a gap it never recorded.

entry.title: The Cambrian Explosion
entry.summary: Live debate. Almost every major animal group appears in the fossil record within about twenty million years. Whether that is an explosion of life or an explosion of fossils is the argument, and it has been running since Darwin apologised for it.

entry.title: The Call of the Void
entry.summary: Documented. Standing at a height, a small number of people feel a sudden urge to jump. It is not a death wish, it is common, and it has a name in French that predates the research.

entry.title: The Boötes Void
entry.summary: Documented. A region of sky about 330 million light years across contains far fewer galaxies than it should. It is real, it is not empty, and it is not evidence of anything stranger than large-scale structure.

entry.title: Blue Light and Circadian Damage
entry.summary: Live debate. Short-wavelength light suppresses melatonin and shifts the body clock. That much is solid. The claim that screens damage the retina, or that blue-blocking glasses fix sleep, is where the evidence thins out.

entry.title: The Black Hole Information Paradox
entry.summary: Live debate. Hawking radiation carries no information about what fell in. If that is true, quantum mechanics is wrong; if it is false, relativity is. Fifty years of work has produced progress and no experiment.

entry.title: The Big Bounce
entry.summary: Live debate. If the universe contracts before it expands, the Big Bang is not a beginning. The idea is mathematically developed and observationally untested, and the cosmic microwave background is where it would show.

entry.title: The Bermuda Triangle
entry.summary: Debunked. Ships and aircraft have been lost in the western Atlantic, as they have been lost everywhere. The triangle was assembled from a handful of famous cases, a bestseller, and an absence of denominator.

entry.title: The Berenstain Bears
entry.summary: Debunked. A generation remembers the books as 'Berenstein'. They were always 'Berenstain'. The spelling is the archive's neatest case of a false memory shared by thousands of people.

entry.title: Ball Lightning
entry.summary: Live debate. Glowing spheres that drift through rooms during thunderstorms have been reported for four centuries, filmed once, and measured spectroscopically in a handful of cases. The reports are too consistent to dismiss and too rare to pin down.

entry.title: The Baghdad Battery
entry.summary: Debunked. A clay jar with a copper cylinder and an iron rod will produce a voltage if you fill it with vinegar. Whether anyone in Parthian Iraq did that is a different question, and the answer is almost certainly no.

entry.title: Baalbek and the Giants
entry.summary: Debunked. The Roman temple platform at Baalbek contains three stones of about 800 tonnes each. They were quarried, moved and set by Roman engineers, and the claim that only giants could have done it is an argument from incredulity with a documented answer.

entry.title: The Baader–Meinhof Effect
entry.summary: Documented. Learn a new word and it appears everywhere for a week. Nothing has changed except your attention — which is why it is also called the frequency illusion.

entry.title: Assembly Theory
entry.summary: Live debate. A proposed measure of how complex an object is, by counting the minimum steps needed to build it. Its authors argue it explains selection and can detect life; its critics argue it measures construction, not causation.

entry.title: Arthur as a Roman Commander
entry.summary: Live debate. The earliest mention of Arthur is a battle list written three centuries after he supposedly lived. The claim that he was a Roman officer is a modern attempt to fill the gap.

entry.title: Archimedes' Heat Ray
entry.summary: Live debate. Mirrors on the walls of Syracuse, focusing sunlight onto Roman ships. The story is late, the physics is marginal, and the experiments have produced smoke and no fire.

entry.title: Aphantasia
entry.summary: Documented. Some people close their eyes and see nothing. The condition was described in 1880, named in 2015, and is now the best-studied example of how differently ordinary minds are furnished.

entry.title: The Anthropocene
entry.summary: Documented. Humans have changed the rock record. Whether that deserves a place in the geological timescale was put to a vote in 2024 and lost — and the vote is more interesting than the answer.

entry.title: The Amber Room
entry.summary: Live debate. A room panelled in amber, looted by the Nazis in 1941, and lost in 1945. The reconstruction is finished; the original is still missing, and the search has produced a great deal of theory and no amber.

entry.title: Alien Hand Syndrome
entry.summary: Documented. A hand that acts on its own — unbuttoning a shirt, grabbing a tool, resisting the other hand — is a real consequence of damage to the connections between the hemispheres.

entry.title: Algorithmic Radicalisation
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim that recommendation systems push people toward extremes. The mechanism is plausible, the evidence is thinner than the headlines, and the platform data that would settle it is not available.

entry.title: The Akashic Records
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A compendium of everything that has ever happened, said to be readable by the trained. It is a claim with no evidence, no mechanism and no test — and it shaped a great deal of modern spiritual writing.

entry.title: The AI Box Experiment
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A person role-plays an AI locked in a text-only box and tries to persuade a gatekeeper to release it. Two claimed successes are cited as evidence that containment would fail. They are anecdotes, not experiments.

entry.title: The Aestivation Hypothesis
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Advanced civilisations may be asleep, waiting for the universe to cool so their computers run more efficiently. It explains the absence of aliens by predicting it, which is either elegant or unfalsifiable.

entry.title: Abiogenic Petroleum
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Oil is not made from fossils in the way schoolbooks imply — but it is organic. The claim that it forms abiotically in the mantle has been tested for a century and has produced no commercial field.

entry.title: The Zoo Hypothesis
entry.summary: Fringe claim. If the galaxy is full of life, why is it quiet? John Ball's 1973 answer was that they are leaving us alone on purpose — treating Earth as a preserve, and waiting for us to grow up.

entry.title: The Younger Dryas Impact
entry.summary: Live debate. The Younger Dryas cooling is real and abrupt. Whether an impact caused it — and whether that impact explains megafaunal extinctions and the Clovis collapse — is where the argument starts.

entry.title: White Holes
entry.summary: Live debate. Run the film backwards and a black hole becomes a white hole: a region nothing can enter, spraying matter outward. The equations permit it. The sky has not shown one.

entry.title: Where Earth’s Water Came From
entry.summary: Live debate. Oceans cover most of the planet, and the planet should have boiled them off while it was forming. Something delivered water afterwards — or it was here all along.

entry.title: The Voynich Manuscript
entry.summary: Live debate. An illustrated book in an unknown script, written on vellum dated to the early fifteenth century. Every generation produces a decipherment. None has survived contact with other scholars.

entry.title: Where Viruses Came From
entry.summary: Live debate. Viruses are not alive by most definitions, and they are the most abundant biological entities on Earth. Where they came from is one of biology's genuinely unresolved questions.

entry.title: Urban Legends & Creepypasta
entry.summary: Live debate. A Photoshop contest produced a monster. Five years later, two twelve-year-olds tried to kill their friend for him. This is the only page in the archive where the fiction caused the harm.

entry.title: Universal Basic Income
entry.summary: Live debate. The strongest argument for a basic income is not that it makes people work more. It is that a welfare state built on conditions and paperwork produces the poverty it claims to fix.

entry.title: Unexplained Phenomena
entry.summary: Live debate. The honest cases. Not ghosts and not cover-ups — events with real evidence, real papers, and conclusions that are still argued.

entry.title: Underwater Worlds
entry.summary: Live debate. More than two-thirds of the seafloor has no modern high-resolution map. That single fact powers an industry of undersea-civilization claims — and it is also the most honest fact on this page.

entry.title: The Turing Test
entry.summary: Live debate. Turing's 1950 paper replaced an unanswerable question with a game: can a machine's text be told from a person's? Seventy-five years later the game is won and the original question is exactly where it was.

entry.title: Turbulence
entry.summary: Open problem. We can land a rocket on a barge using models of turbulent flow. We cannot prove that the equations describing it always have smooth solutions.

entry.title: Time Paradoxes
entry.summary: Live debate. Kill your grandfather and you were never born; travel back and give yourself the idea you got from yourself. These paradoxes are not puzzles about fiction. They are what happens when you take the equations of relativity seriously.

entry.title: Time Crystals
entry.summary: Documented. An ordinary crystal repeats in space. A time crystal repeats in time, indefinitely, without consuming energy — and unlike a pendulum, it does so in its ground state.

entry.title: The Thucydides Trap
entry.summary: Live debate. Thucydides said the war between Athens and Sparta came from 'the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta'. Allison turned that sentence into a dataset.

entry.title: Theranos
entry.summary: Documented. One drop of blood, two hundred tests, a black box. The machine did not work, the tests ran on other companies' equipment, and the board did not include a single haematologist.

entry.title: Technological Unemployment
entry.summary: Live debate. Every generation has been told that machines will end work, and every generation has been mostly wrong. That history is an argument, not a guarantee.

entry.title: Tartarus, the Pit
entry.summary: Documented. “As far beneath the earth as heaven is above it.” The Greeks gave the underworld a floor plan, a wall, a gate and a prisoner list. Everything after that is reuse.

entry.title: Tartaria & the Mud Flood
entry.summary: Debunked. Every old city has basement windows cut in half by the pavement. The theory says a civilisation of giants built the buildings, then a wall of mud buried the ground floors and the history books.

entry.title: Tabby’s Star
entry.summary: Live debate. A star 1,470 light years away keeps dimming in strange, uneven ways. A comet swarm was the first guess, dust the current one — and a megastructure was never more than a headline.

entry.title: Supersymmetry
entry.summary: Live debate. A symmetry between matter and force particles would solve several problems at once. The LHC was built partly to find it, and has found nothing. That is not the same as ruling it out.

entry.title: Superrationality
entry.summary: Fringe claim. In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma with a stranger, defecting is dominant. Unless the stranger is your mirror — in which case the choice is not what to do, but what kind of reasoner to be.

entry.title: Room-Temperature Superconductivity
entry.summary: Live debate. A material that carries current with no resistance would rebuild the electrical grid. The physics is real; the room-temperature claims have not survived.

entry.title: Dual Suns, Dual Stars
entry.summary: Live debate. The Sun has no companion today. That is a measurement, not an opinion — and yet the “second sun” idea is one of the most persistent in fringe cosmology, because it is half right.

entry.title: Substrate Independence
entry.summary: Live debate. Functionalism says a mind is defined by what it does, not what it is made of — so the same program would be conscious wherever it ran. That is either obvious or a category error, and the disagreement is about which.

entry.title: Strings versus Loops
entry.summary: Live debate. Two research programmes, one target: a theory of gravity that works at the Planck scale. They disagree about almost everything else, and neither has been tested.

entry.title: The Stoned Ape
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Human brains tripled in size because our ancestors ate psilocybin mushrooms, which rewired us into language, art and self-reflection. It is a wonderful story with a real pharmacology and almost no archaeology.

entry.title: Stochastic Parrots or World Models
entry.summary: Live debate. One camp says a language model is a curve-fitting machine that parrots its training data. The other says that to predict text well enough, it has to build a model of the world that produced it.

entry.title: The Space Elevator
entry.summary: Live debate. Tsiolkovsky proposed it in 1895 after seeing the Eiffel Tower. Arthur C. Clarke made it famous in 1979. It remains the cheapest imaginable way to orbit and the least available, for one reason: the material.

entry.title: The Electromagnetic Soul
entry.summary: Fringe claim. “The soul is an electromagnetic pattern; the body is hardware.” It sounds like physics. It is a metaphor wearing a lab coat — and the real measurements are more interesting than the metaphor.

entry.title: Sonoluminescence
entry.summary: Live debate. Sound makes a bubble collapse; the collapse emits a flash of light lasting picoseconds. The inside may be hotter than the surface of the Sun, and nobody can measure it directly.

entry.title: Snowball Earth
entry.summary: Documented. Twice in the Neoproterozoic, ice reached sea level in the tropics. The evidence is in the rocks and is not seriously disputed; how the planet got out again is still argued about.

entry.title: The Simulation Hypothesis
entry.summary: Live debate. Bostrom's argument is not “we are probably simulated”. It is a trilemma, and one of the three horns is boring. The internet took the exciting horn and dropped the rest.

entry.title: The Simpsons Predictions
entry.summary: Live debate. The show has run for more than 750 episodes of jokes about the future. People remember the ones that landed. Here is the whole list, checked episode by episode, with the ones that did not land.

entry.title: The Silurian Hypothesis
entry.summary: Documented. If an industrial civilisation lived on Earth 60 million years ago, would we know? Two astrophysicists asked the question properly — and the answer says more about us than about them.

entry.title: Who Wrote Shakespeare?
entry.summary: Debunked. A glovemaker's son from Warwickshire could not have written those plays — so runs the argument, and it has been running since 1856. The documents say otherwise, and they are duller than the conspiracy.

entry.title: Secular Stagnation
entry.summary: Live debate. If the interest rate that balances saving and investment is below zero, the central bank cannot reach it. Demand then falls short year after year, and the economy runs cool not because of a shock but because of its structure.

entry.title: Secret Tests
entry.summary: Documented. A city sprayed with bacteria, dead infants measured for fallout, a cat with a transmitter in its skull, a gun that causes heart attacks, and a proposal to make soldiers attracted to each other. All real documents.

entry.title: Secret Societies
entry.summary: Documented. The Illuminati existed for about ten years, was banned, had its papers seized and published — and has been running the world ever since, according to people who have never read the papers.

entry.title: Screen Time and Teen Mental Health
entry.summary: Live debate. Two camps, one dataset, opposite headlines. The honest summary is that screen use correlates weakly with well-being, that the correlation is smaller than nearly everything else in the same data, and that causality is unresolved.

entry.title: Scarcity or Ingenuity
entry.summary: Live debate. The bet was $1,000 on five metals over ten years. Simon won, Ehrlich paid, and the argument has continued as if the bet had not happened.

entry.title: Scaling Laws
entry.summary: Live debate. Double the parameters and the loss drops by a predictable amount, across seven orders of magnitude. Then the awkward part: loss is not capability, and the smooth curves stop being smooth.

entry.title: Roko's Basilisk
entry.summary: Fringe claim. A future AI will torture anyone who knew it was coming and did nothing to help. You have now read about it. That last sentence is the entire mechanism.

entry.title: The Lost Colony
entry.summary: Live debate. 115 English colonists, a word carved on a post, and four centuries of stories about vanishing. The likeliest answer is that they did not vanish at all.

entry.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
entry.summary: Open problem. One vertical line in the complex plane decides how evenly the primes are spread. Ten trillion zeros agree. Nobody can prove it, and nobody serious thinks it is false.

entry.title: The Resource Curse
entry.summary: Live debate. Saudi Arabia and Nigeria both sit on enormous oil reserves. One has a GDP per head around twenty times the other. The difference is not geology.

entry.title: Readiness Potentials and Free Will
entry.summary: Live debate. In 1983 Benjamin Libet measured a slow build-up of brain activity starting a few hundred milliseconds before subjects reported deciding to move. It has been cited as proof that free will is an illusion ever since.

entry.title: Rational Choice Voting
entry.summary: Live debate. Downs noticed in 1957 that a self-interested voter should stay home. Sixty years of research has produced four kinds of answer, and no consensus on which one describes actual voters.

entry.title: Quantum Oddities
entry.summary: Live debate. Two of the strangest things physicists have said about electrons and death: you can never experience your own, and there may only be one electron in the universe.

entry.title: Quantum Darwinism
entry.summary: Live debate. Why do we and the environment agree about what a measurement found? Quantum Darwinism answers: because the environment keeps many copies, and only some states get copied.

entry.title: Quantum Advantage
entry.summary: Live debate. In 2019 a quantum processor finished a sampling task in minutes that would take a classical supercomputer millennia. Within five years, classical methods had closed much of the gap.

entry.title: Punctuated Equilibrium
entry.summary: Live debate. The fossil record shows long stretches of nothing followed by sudden change. Whether that is how evolution works, or how rocks record it, is still argued.

entry.title: Proven Conspiracies
entry.summary: Documented. Real conspiracies exist, and they are on the record. That is precisely why the unfalsifiable ones are recognisable: they look nothing like this.

entry.title: Prophecies
entry.summary: Live debate. The world has ended, on schedule, hundreds of times. The interesting question is not why the predictions fail — it is what the believers do on the Monday afterwards.

entry.title: Primordial Black Holes
entry.summary: Live debate. If the early universe was dense enough, it could have collapsed into black holes smaller than atoms. Some of them might still be here — and might be the missing mass.

entry.title: Planet Nine
entry.summary: Live debate. A handful of icy bodies beyond Neptune share an odd alignment. Either a planet five to ten times Earth's mass shepherds them, or the solar system is playing a statistical trick.

entry.title: The Placebo Effect
entry.summary: Live debate. The placebo effect is real, modest, and much narrower than either its critics or its enthusiasts claim. It works best on symptoms you have to report and worst on outcomes a machine measures.

entry.title: The Pixar Theory
entry.summary: Documented. Every Pixar film is one timeline: animals gain intelligence, humans leave for the machines, and Boo grows up to be the witch in Brave. It is the most elaborate act of fan reading ever assembled — and it never claims to be evidence.

entry.title: Pilot-Wave Theory
entry.summary: Live debate. Bohmian mechanics says the electron really is somewhere, and the wavefunction really does push it. Every experimental prediction matches ordinary quantum theory, because the maths is the same.

entry.title: Phosphine on Venus
entry.summary: Live debate. One absorption line, 20 parts per billion, and a gas that on Earth is made by life. The follow-up work has been brutal — and the story is not quite over.

entry.title: Phantom Time
entry.summary: Debunked. Charlemagne never existed, and 297 years of the early Middle Ages were invented by two men who wanted to live in the year 1000. It is a seductive story, and dendrochronology alone ends it.

entry.title: Peto's Paradox
entry.summary: Live debate. A blue whale has a thousand times more cells than you. By the arithmetic of random mutation, it should die of cancer almost immediately. It lives a century.

entry.title: Pegasus
entry.summary: Documented. No link to tap, no app to install. A crafted message arrives and the phone is compromised — journalists, lawyers, activists and heads of state on the list.

entry.title: Paul Is Dead
entry.summary: Debunked. In 1966 Paul McCartney died in a car crash and the Beatles replaced him with a lookalike, hiding clues in their album covers. The man himself has been asked about it for fifty years.

entry.title: Panpsychism
entry.summary: Live debate. The view that experience is a basic feature of matter, not something that emerges from complexity. It is taken seriously by a minority of philosophers, has no test, and is not the same as saying rocks are conscious.

entry.title: The Panama Papers
entry.summary: Documented. Eleven and a half million files from one law firm. The scandal was not that everyone was breaking the law — it was how much of the world's wealth was routed where nobody could see it.

entry.title: ‘Oumuamua
entry.summary: Live debate. It came from outside the solar system, tumbled, had no visible tail, and sped up slightly on the way out. Every natural explanation has a problem, which is why it became famous.

entry.title: The Origin of Life
entry.summary: Live debate. Life began once, four billion years ago, and left no fossils. Every account of how is an inference from chemistry — which is why several can be true at once, in sequence.

entry.title: Open versus Closed Models
entry.summary: Live debate. A closed model can be withdrawn. An open one cannot. That single asymmetry drives most of the argument, and neither side disputes it.

entry.title: The Omega Point
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Pierre Teilhard de Chardin imagined evolution converging on a collective consciousness he called the Omega Point. Frank Tipler gave it an equation — and the equation needs a universe that is not going to collapse.

entry.title: Objective Collapse
entry.summary: Live debate. Standard quantum theory says the wavefunction collapses when measured, and never says what a measurement is. Objective-collapse models replace that with real physics: the collapse happens on its own.

entry.title: Oak Island
entry.summary: Debunked. A depression in the ground, a story about pirate gold, and 230 years of men bankrupting themselves to find it. The pit is real. The treasure is the part nobody has produced.

entry.title: Unknown Mysteries
entry.summary: Live debate. Two case studies in how a mystery is manufactured: a loose boundary, a good story, a bestseller — and then, thirty years later, the paperwork.

entry.title: Mutants & “Superpowers”
entry.summary: Documented. There are people whose bones will not break, people who can see a colour you cannot, and populations that function where visitors vomit and lose consciousness. None of them glow.

entry.title: The Muon's Wobble
entry.summary: Live debate. For twenty years the muon's magnetic moment looked like the cleanest crack in the Standard Model. Then a different way of doing the hardest part of the calculation closed the gap.

entry.title: The End of Moore’s Law
entry.summary: Live debate. Moore's law was an observation about economics that became a schedule the industry organised itself around. Its end is not the end of computing; it is the end of a very specific kind of free progress.

entry.title: How the Moon Formed
entry.summary: Live debate. A Mars-sized body hit the young Earth and the debris became the Moon. The broad picture is accepted; the isotope evidence has been making it complicated for twenty years.

entry.title: MOND
entry.summary: Live debate. One constant, 10⁻¹⁰ metres per second squared, and a rule: below that acceleration, gravity pulls harder than Newton says. It fits galaxies beautifully and clusters badly.

entry.title: Modern Monetary Theory
entry.summary: Live debate. A government that borrows in a currency it prints can always pay. That is arithmetic, not ideology. What follows from it — and what does not — is where the fight is.

entry.title: Minimum Wage Effects
entry.summary: Live debate. New Jersey raised its minimum wage in 1992 and Pennsylvania did not. The study that compared them overturned a textbook, and every study since has been arguing with it.

entry.title: The Median Voter Theorem
entry.summary: Live debate. Duncan Black proved in 1948 that majority voting on a single dimension picks the median voter's preference. Downs applied it to parties in 1957. The prediction is convergence, and the last forty years of American politics is the counter-example.

entry.title: Mass Hysteria
entry.summary: Documented. Four hundred people danced until they collapsed in Strasbourg in 1518. The municipal records survive. This is the best-documented case in history of a symptom spreading through a crowd faster than any pathogen.

entry.title: Market Efficiency
entry.summary: Live debate. If prices already contain all available information, nobody can beat the market except by luck. Half a century of tests has produced both support and a list of exceptions that refuse to go away.

entry.title: Many Worlds
entry.summary: Documented. This is the one entry in the archive that is not a fringe claim at all. It is a serious, taught, published interpretation of quantum mechanics — and it still does not mean what the internet says it means.

entry.title: The Mandela Effect
entry.summary: Live debate. A large group of people remember the same wrong thing. It is either evidence of a parallel universe, or the most ordinary fact about human memory there is.

entry.title: Magnetoreception
entry.summary: Documented. Animals navigate by the Earth's magnetic field. That much is settled by decades of behavioural experiments. How a biological cell measures a field a hundred thousand times weaker than a fridge magnet is not.

entry.title: Magnetic Monopoles
entry.summary: Live debate. Cut a magnet in half and you get two magnets. Nobody has ever found an isolated north pole. That absence is one of the most informative null results in physics.

entry.title: MAD Stability
entry.summary: Live debate. Mutual assured destruction is the most consequential theory ever adopted without a controlled test. It has one data point in its favour and dozens of near-failures against.

entry.title: Lost Continents
entry.summary: Live debate. Lemuria was invented to explain where lemurs came from. Within twenty years it was a civilisation of telepathic giants who kept dinosaurs as pets. The real drowned continents are stranger in a quieter way.

entry.title: The Lindy Effect
entry.summary: Live debate. At Lindy's delicatessen in New York, comedians believed a joke that had lasted a week would last another week. Mandelbrot gave the observation a name; Taleb gave it a following.

entry.title: Learning Styles
entry.summary: Debunked. The idea that children learn better when taught in their preferred mode — visual, auditory, kinaesthetic — is one of the most widely held beliefs in education and one of the most thoroughly tested negatives in psychology.

entry.title: Lead and Crime
entry.summary: Live debate. Violent crime fell through the 1990s in every rich country at once, and nobody predicted it. One explanation is that a generation stopped breathing leaded petrol as children.

entry.title: Last Thursdayism
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The universe was created last Thursday, complete with your memories, the fossils, and this website. It is not a claim anyone believes. It is a machine for showing what evidence cannot do.

entry.title: The Larger Globe
entry.summary: Live debate. “Larger globe” is not one theory. It is at least three, with different inventors, different evidence and different fates.

entry.title: Kardashev Bottlenecks
entry.summary: Live debate. If growth continues at any plausible rate, the Milky Way is a few tens of millions of years of work. The galaxy is 13 billion years old. The silence is a statement about bottlenecks.

entry.title: The Jevons Paradox
entry.summary: Live debate. In 1865 William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines increased Britain's coal consumption, not reduced it. The pattern has been embarrassing energy policy ever since.

entry.title: Inflation versus a Bounce
entry.summary: Live debate. Inflation is the standard answer to 'why is the universe so uniform?' — and it is also the theory its critics say can explain almost anything, which is the problem.

entry.title: IIT versus Global Workspace
entry.summary: Live debate. One theory says consciousness is integrated information, wherever it occurs. The other says it is information broadcast widely in the brain. Both made predictions, and both were tested.

entry.title: Beyond the Ice Wall
entry.summary: Debunked. If the world continues past Antarctica, the continent is not a continent but a boundary — and the treaty that governs it becomes a cover story.

entry.title: Hyperloop Feasibility
entry.summary: Live debate. The white paper was 57 pages of enthusiasm. The hard parts were not the magnets; they were the tube, the thermal expansion, the safety case and the fact that a train needs to carry enough people to pay for itself.

entry.title: The Hubble Tension
entry.summary: Live debate. Measure the expansion of the universe nearby and you get 73. Measure it in the early universe and you get 67. Both teams are careful, both error bars are small, and the gap is now five sigma.

entry.title: The Holographic Principle
entry.summary: Live debate. The information in a volume of space can be encoded on its boundary. In one kind of universe, this has been demonstrated. Whether it applies to ours is open.

entry.title: Hollow Earth & the Inner Sun
entry.summary: Fringe claim. The shell has an 800-mile wall. The polar openings are 1,400 miles wide. There is a small sun in the middle, and someone has always just come back from there.

entry.title: Did Hitler Escape?
entry.summary: Debunked. A U-boat to Argentina, a Nazi compound in Patagonia, a death staged in the bunker. The story has books, documentaries and declassified FBI files. It does not have a body that matches.

entry.title: The Gut–Brain Axis
entry.summary: Live debate. Gut bacteria talk to the brain, and the brain talks back. The question is how much of the conversation changes disease, and how much is a passenger effect.

entry.title: Growth Mindset
entry.summary: Live debate. Believing that ability can grow is a defensible idea with a small, real effect. Believing it is a lever that raises attainment for everyone is a claim that failed its largest test.

entry.title: The Great Stagnation
entry.summary: Live debate. The postwar generation got antibiotics, electrification, cars and mass higher education. Since 1970 the measurable productivity dividend has been much thinner — or the measurement has stopped counting what matters.

entry.title: The Great Filter
entry.summary: Live debate. The silence has to mean something. Either the hard step is behind us and we are lucky, or it is ahead of us and we are early.

entry.title: Göbekli Tepe
entry.summary: Live debate. Carved pillars, sixteen tonnes each, built by people without pottery or farming. The date is settled. What the enclosures were for is not.

entry.title: Giants
entry.summary: Debunked. There is a race of giants in the oldest stories we have. There is also a ten-foot gypsum corpse in a New York field, sold for $23,000, and a mastodon thigh-bone that looked like a man.

entry.title: The Giant Trees
entry.summary: Debunked. Devils Tower does look like a stump. It has vertical grain, a flat top and a flared base. It is also made of a rock that trees cannot make.

entry.title: Geographic Determinism
entry.summary: Live debate. Eurasia has more domesticable plants, more large animals and a long east–west axis. That is true and important. Whether it explains which countries are rich today is another question.

entry.title: Gaia
entry.summary: Live debate. The Earth regulates its own temperature, chemistry and atmosphere as if it were alive. The strong version is wrong, the weak version is now mainstream, and the argument between them created Earth system science.

entry.title: Fusion on the Grid
entry.summary: Live debate. In December 2022 the National Ignition Facility got more energy out of a fusion target than the laser delivered. Headlines said fusion had arrived. The grid is still waiting.

entry.title: FTX
entry.summary: Documented. Billions in customer deposits were lent to a trading firm run by the founder's girlfriend, moved through code exemptions, and spent on venture bets and real estate.

entry.title: The Free Energy Principle
entry.summary: Live debate. A single mathematical principle is said to explain perception, action, learning and life itself. Its defenders call it the closest thing neuroscience has to a unifying law; its critics call it unfalsifiable, and both have a point.

entry.title: Noah, Gilgamesh & the Great Flood
entry.summary: Live debate. A man builds a boat, loads the animals, and the world is drowned. The story is older than the Bible, and the geology is younger than the story.

entry.title: Flat Earth & the Firmament
entry.summary: Debunked. A disc with the North Pole at the centre, a wall of ice at the rim, and a dome overhead. The model is simple. What is interesting is how it survives.

entry.title: The Firewall Paradox
entry.summary: Live debate. In 2012 four physicists showed that a falling observer at a black-hole horizon cannot both see empty space and preserve quantum information. The field has been arguing about which assumption to give up ever since.

entry.title: Fast Radio Bursts
entry.summary: Documented. Millisecond flashes of radio energy from other galaxies, first dismissed as a microwave oven and now observed in their thousands. The phenomenon is documented; the source of most of them is still open.

entry.title: The First Eukaryote
entry.summary: Live debate. Every animal, plant and fungus descends from a cell that swallowed a bacterium and kept it. The swallowing is certain; the swallow-er is not.

entry.title: Enshittification
entry.summary: Documented. First the platform is good to you, then it is good to its business customers, then it is good to nobody but its shareholders. The pattern is real; the law is not.

entry.title: Ego Depletion
entry.summary: Debunked. For fifteen years, 'willpower is a finite resource like a battery' was textbook psychology, complete with the advice to drink sugar water. Then the replications came back near zero.

entry.title: The Egg
entry.summary: Documented. Every person who has ever lived is you, living every life in turn. It is a short story by the man who wrote The Martian — and the internet turned it into a theory.

entry.title: The Ediacaran Organisms
entry.summary: Live debate. For decades, the Ediacaran fossils were a taxonomic orphanage: too big to be microbes, too weird to be animals. Molecular evidence has now placed some of them, without settling the group.

entry.title: Echo Chambers
entry.summary: Live debate. The theory is intuitive: recommendation systems show you what you already agree with, and you drift outward. The experiments that changed people's feeds found the drift was smaller than expected — and not always in the predicted direction.

entry.title: Dyson Swarms
entry.summary: Live debate. A solid shell around a star is gravitationally impossible. A swarm of collectors is not, and the difference matters: the swarm is the version astronomers actually search for.

entry.title: Dyatlov Pass
entry.summary: Documented. Nine experienced ski hikers cut their way out of a tent in the night and died in the snow. Sixty years later, two physicists modelled the snow and closed most of the gap.

entry.title: Dunbar's Number
entry.summary: Live debate. Dunbar plotted neocortex size against group size across primates and extrapolated to humans: about 150 stable relationships. Armies, firms and villages seemed to fit. Then the statistics were redone.

entry.title: Dragons & Dinosaurs
entry.summary: Live debate. Every culture on Earth independently invented a giant reptile. In 2013, a team tried to work out whether they did it independently at all.

entry.title: The Doomsday Argument
entry.summary: Fringe claim. You were born somewhere in the human sequence, not at a special point in it. Apply that assumption and the numbers say the species probably ends within a few thousand years. The argument turns entirely on whether the assumption is legitimate.

entry.title: Unresolved Disappearances
entry.summary: Live debate. A ship found sailing itself, a pilot who vanished over an ocean, five children who left no remains. These are the cases where the evidence ran out rather than pointed somewhere.

entry.title: The Dinosaur Extinction
entry.summary: Documented. An asteroid hit the Yucatán 66 million years ago and three quarters of species died. The argument about whether the impact or the Deccan volcanoes did it is now mostly an argument about timing, and the timing has been measured.

entry.title: Democratic Peace
entry.summary: Live debate. Kant predicted it in 1795. Statistical work from the 1960s found it. Democracies fight plenty of wars — just not, on the whole, each other — and the explanation matters enormously for policy.

entry.title: Deep Web & Dark Web
entry.summary: Documented. Ninety per cent of the web is “deep” in the most boring possible sense: it is behind a login, a paywall, or a search box. The dark web is a small encrypted subset of that, and it is not a place.

entry.title: The Dead Internet Theory
entry.summary: Live debate. The claim: most of the internet is no longer people. The data does not support the total version — and the partial version is genuinely unsettling.

entry.title: Dark Matter
entry.summary: Live debate. The case that something invisible holds galaxies together is overwhelming. The case for any particular particle is not — and that gap is where the field currently lives.

entry.title: The Dark Forest
entry.summary: Live debate. The universe is a dark forest full of armed hunters. Make a sound, and something finds you. It is the most chilling answer to “where is everybody?” — and it was written as a novel.

entry.title: Curses
entry.summary: Debunked. One curse has been checked with epidemiology, one was dismantled in a courtroom, and one was invented by a newspaper in 1908. All three are still going.

entry.title: Cryptids
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Cryptozoology has one legitimate test — produce the animal — and one recurring problem: the most famous photograph in the field was confessed to be a toy submarine.

entry.title: Creationism and the Alternatives to Darwin
entry.summary: Live debate. Common ancestry is about as well supported as anything in science. How evolution works in detail is still argued about — by biologists. This page separates the two, claim by claim, without pretending the argument is even.

entry.title: The Contact Hypothesis
entry.summary: Live debate. Intergroup contact reduces prejudice — one of the most replicated findings in social psychology. The dispute is about the conditions: equal status, shared goals, cooperation and institutional support, all of which are easy to state and hard to arrange.

entry.title: Cold Fusion
entry.summary: Fringe claim. Two electrochemists announced tabletop fusion on 23 March 1989. Within six months the effect had failed to replicate, and thirty-seven years later there is still a conference, a journal and no accepted mechanism.

entry.title: The Chinese Room
entry.summary: Live debate. A person in a room follows rules for manipulating Chinese characters and produces perfect answers in Chinese. She understands nothing. Is the room a computer, or is this a story about what it feels like to be one?

entry.title: Broken Windows Policing
entry.summary: Live debate. An essay in The Atlantic in 1982 argued that untended disorder invites serious crime. It became the operating theory of American policing, and then it was tested.

entry.title: The Bosnian Pyramids
entry.summary: Debunked. Four hills near Visoko, said to be the largest human-made pyramids on Earth, older than Sumer. The shape is real. The construction is not.

entry.title: Boltzmann Brains
entry.summary: Live debate. If the universe fluctuates forever, a random self-aware brain with false memories is far more likely than an entire ordered cosmos. Nobody thinks that means you are one. It means something is wrong with the model.

entry.title: Black Swans
entry.summary: Live debate. Nobody predicted 2008, the pandemic or the smartphone. The interesting question is not that surprises happen but whether our models are built to be surprised by them.

entry.title: The Black Knight
entry.summary: Debunked. An alien satellite in polar orbit for 13,000 years, photographed by NASA in 1998. The photograph is real. The object is a piece of insulation that drifted out of the shuttle's cargo bay.

entry.title: Bitcoin as Digital Gold
entry.summary: Live debate. The white paper proposed a peer-to-peer electronic cash system. Fifteen years later its main use is as an asset whose price is quoted in the currency it was meant to replace.

entry.title: The Bicameral Mind
entry.summary: Live debate. Three thousand years ago, humans had no inner life. Their own thoughts arrived as the voices of gods, and they obeyed them. It is one of the most audacious books of the century, and the neuroscience does not support it.
